# P R E F A C E .

I present to the Public the Translation of a Greek Manuscript which was found in the Library of a foreign Nation, extremely jealous of this kind of treasure <note>original: "thréfor." It was a popular literary device in the 1700s to claim a story was a "found manuscript" to give the narrative an air of ancient authority and exotic mystery.</note>. Those who procured for me the reading of this Manuscript, only permitted me to publish it by translating it, without indicating the Library to which the Original belongs. The Author is not named anywhere: but some parts of the Book itself make it known that he was a Greek by origin, living in Alexandria <note>A Mediterranean port city in Egypt, Alexandria was the greatest center of Greek learning and culture in the ancient world.</note> under the Empire of Marcus Aurelius <note>Roman Emperor from 161 to 180 AD, known as a Stoic philosopher and the last of the "Five Good Emperors."</note>.

There is no reason to doubt that this is a Work of fiction <term>fiction: a "roman" or work of imagination, often contrasted with "history" in the 18th century</term>. The enterprises whose successes are roughly such as the Reader desires,

*The Travels of Cyrus* <note>Original: *Voyages de Cyrus*. This was a popular philosophical novel by Andrew Michael Ramsay, published in 1727, which followed the model of Fénelon's *Telemachus* by using a fictionalized historical journey to impart political and moral wisdom.</note> are, in accordance with their title, nothing more than a journey undertaken by the Hero to gather instructions from all the Sages of his time; and to bring back to his States what was good & advantageous in the different Laws of celebrated Kingdoms or Republics.

The Work concerned here is of the same genre as both of them regarding its moral purpose; but it differs from them in form even more than they differ from each other. Both are properly an Education: & although *Cyrus* emerges from it less young than *Telemachus*; the two Heroes have as yet only gathered the instructions that they were to put into use; or have only made attempts at what they were to practice; the former in the conduct of a small Kingdom, and the latter in the government of a great Empire. ->PREFACE.<-

his honor <note>Original: "son honneur", completing the phrase from the previous page.</note> in sacrificing his interests to them, and which make a duty for him out of the happiness he procures for them.

It is not only by natural disposition or by habit that Sethos is virtuous. The motives for his conduct are drawn from constant and enlightened principles which he displays on various occasions; and he makes decisions for himself which, while always tending toward the most perfect and even the heroic, are nonetheless more commendable for their soundness than for their severity. From this, one must judge that the Author, who lived in the second century <note>The book *Sethos* (1731) was a "pseudo-translation"—the real author, Abbé Jean Terrasson, claimed he was merely translating an ancient Greek manuscript from the 2nd century to give the story more authority.</note>, had some knowledge of a morality far superior to that of Paganism <term>Paganism: In this context, the term refers to the ancient polytheistic religions of Greece, Rome, and Egypt, which 18th-century writers often viewed as morally "incomplete" compared to later philosophical or religious systems.</term>. # BOOK I.

A 2
<meta>catchword: reign</meta>

* The other Egyptian Dynasties <note>A dynasty refers to a sequence of rulers from the same family or line.</note>, which some historians count as roughly twenty from the time of Menes until the reign of Sesostris, are merely specific branches of those four primary lineages. The different names assigned to them—such as the Heracleopolitans, the Xoites, the Elephantines, and others—arise only from the fact that certain Kings within each Dynasty resided in different capital cities within the same Kingdom.

Regarding the Shepherd Kings <term>Rois Pasteurs: Historically known as the Hyksos, these were foreign rulers of likely Semitic origin who controlled Lower and Middle Egypt for several generations.</term> who were foreigners, and whose presence in Egypt for three or four centuries appears to have interrupted the royal succession; they never held stable territory beyond Tanis at the edge of the Nile Delta. They forced the native Kings to retreat to Heliopolis <note>Heliopolis, the "City of the Sun," was one of the oldest cities in ancient Egypt and a major religious center.</note>. However, because these foreigners, who originally came from Arabia, made frequent raids into the rest of Egypt, the Egyptians eventually united to attack and defeat them. As a result, those conquered by the Egyptians and their descendants provided the whole of Egypt with a source of slaves. 

This victory was achieved nearly two hundred years before the birth of Sesostris <note>Sesostris is a legendary king of Egypt often identified with the historical Pharaoh Senusret I or Senusret III, though the author treats him as a singular heroic figure.</note>, who found Egypt in a state of peace and led it to a period of great prosperity. This Hero raised his own courage by following the example of the God Osiris. According to Egyptian traditions, Osiris had traveled across much of the earth to teach humanity how to cultivate the land and how to form kind and productive societies. Under the late King, he had risen not through all the formal titles one might hold, but through every position of trust <term>commissions de confiance|Specific assignments granted based on personal merit and royal trust rather than hereditary rank</term> with which one can be charged, whether in war, in negotiations, or in the internal administration of a Kingdom.

He himself advised the Queen—just as he had requested of the late King—not to reveal to the Public the honor she bestowed upon him; for fear of exciting the jealousy of the Great <note>Referring to the high-ranking nobility or "les Grands."</note> and the inevitable murmuring of the People against even the ministers most devoted to the public happiness. Thus the Queen, keeping Amedès as a secret advisor under an unassuming title, otherwise chose the best Subjects from among those whose various ranks of birth seemed to make them candidates for each of the positions that needed to be filled. By these means, sovereign authority was used to distinguish merit without overturning the social order; and the malcontents were but a small number of people who did not even dare to vent complaints that the public voice would not have supported.

While the Queen devoted herself entirely to the affairs of State, the King gave himself over to all the amusements of a brilliant Court. But as these pleasures never followed any serious occupations, they barely saved him from boredom; they revealed in the King of a great People a man to whom his own leisure was a burden. Among the women who surrounded him, there was one named Daluca, the childless widow of a high-ranking Lord of the Court. She had passed the age where women take care of their beauty only for the sake of romance <note>original: "la galanterie"; in this 18th-century context, it refers to the social play of flirtation and courtship common in royal circles.</note>; she was entering the age where they think to use what remains of it to serve their ambition. She formed a plan to make herself mistress of the King's mind. The esteem and respect held for the Queen had deterred all others from such a design. Even Daluca, who understood Osoroth’s temperament <term>génie|Here meaning his specific character, disposition, or mental state</term> perfectly, was careful not to say anything against Nephté that might stir up a disagreeable agitation in his mind. She contented herself with occupying his every moment; she made an art of pleasing through attentiveness and compliance—qualities far more powerful over Kings of a certain age than youth and beauty devoid of conduct or vision. Thus, it was not difficult for her to win the favor of a Prince who resisted nothing. She had perhaps already conceived higher hopes, having noticed that the Queen's health was not strong. But without giving up on a more distant fortune, it was enough for her vanity at that time to be a notable figure for the Courtiers, and to hold a position of some status alongside the Queen.

-> A 6 <-

Nephté, by the dignity of her person and by the very nature of her situation, was far above the anxieties that usually trouble those who feel they hold only a borrowed power <note>original: "pouvoir emprunté"; this refers to delegated authority held at the whim of a monarch, rather than sovereign power held by right.</note>. Thus, although she soon perceived the maneuvers and intrigues of her rival, she feared no personal misfortune; but her foresight alarmed her on behalf of her son. He was only eight years old, and she saw with sorrow that if she were to fail him <note>meaning if she were to die</note> before his father had secured his succession to the Crown, the fate of this young Prince would be left to the reckless Daluca. In Egypt, the eldest sons were the natural heirs to the Throne; yet the father's choice carried great weight, and History provided more than one example of a second or third son being preferred over the first. Sometimes this uncertainty had even given rise to quarrels between brothers, which were decided only by the force of arms. Thus, although the Queen then had no premonition of illness, the thought of an uncertain future threw her into a state of unease. This is why, commending her son through the Priests to all the Divinities of Egypt, she applied herself even more rigorously to her duties, in order to persuade Heaven to favor intentions as legitimate as her own. But the true reward of the righteous lies only in the bosom of the Gods, who do not always favor them in the course of this mortal life.

The Queen's constant dedication, a workload that exceeded the strength of her constitution <term>tempérament|Referring to the 18th-century medical understanding of a person's physical and mental makeup</term>, and perhaps even an excessive fear of falling ill, eventually caused her an indisposition that was slight at first,

In any event, these Physicians, truly accomplished in their Art, employed regarding the Queen everything that their reading, reflections, and experiences could suggest to them. They treated her at first according to the ancient rules, which were prescribed to them under penalty of death: for any Physician who deviated from them answered for his patient; and in case of failure, the death of one surely entailed the death of the other <note>According to historical accounts by Diodorus Siculus, Egyptian doctors were required to follow the "Sacred Books." But the keen interest they felt for the preservation of a Queen such as Nephté, and the groans of an entire People who recommended to them their Sovereign—whom they called their Mother—soon engaged them to seek some new remedies. They disguised them, in truth, under ancient names, whereby they found means to authorize them through some of the innumerable examples with which their books were filled. They even took turns standing at the Palace gate to listen to anyone who might have advice to propose for the Queen's cure. They would then judge these in their private consultations. But it was important for them in such a delicate situation to follow, at least in part, an ancient custom according to which many would place their sick before the doors of their houses, in order to inquire of passersby if they had any remedies for the illness in question <note>This custom is famously described by the historian Herodotus; it allowed the community to share collective medical knowledge when formal medicine failed.</note>.

But of what use are temples, and all the vows made within them, against the decrees issued by the Gods? The Queen, though she submissively followed every order of the physicians, declined from day to day. The most potent remedies—administered even before she reached her final extremity, so as to take advantage of what strength she had left—seemed to have no more effect than ordinary medicines. Her physicians, who would have been less alarmed by sudden, extraordinary crises than by the steady, imperceptible decline they observed in her, never allowed a single word of hope to escape them. The Queen, therefore, resigning herself to her fate, finally resolved to send for a consultation on behalf of her son to the oldest Oracle in the world, located near Memphis. ### BOOK I.

B 2

of the underworld, the gates of the Sun. <note>The author refers to the mythological concept of the *Pylai Heliou* (Gates of the Sun), which in Homeric tradition and Egyptian belief marked the entrance to the realm of the dead.</note> The twelve immense palaces it contained represented, according to their intention, all of Egypt. This is why they had all designated their own burial places there, along with those of their successors in the subterranean chambers. However, the popular imagination—sustained by the ceremonies performed by the Priests before introducing the body into these somber dwellings where few living men had ever entered—had added much to the reality of the place. It was a tenet of their religion to believe that the innumerable winding paths (which, in truth, did fill these underground levels) led the good Kings to a place of delight; whereas the very entrance to the labyrinth was forbidden to Tyrants.

Indeed, as soon as the body reached the banks of a lake called Charon <note>While "Charon" is famously the Greek name for the ferryman of the Styx, the author suggests here that the name is also applied to the lake itself in the Egyptian context.</note>, which had to be crossed to reach the gate of the infernal Gods, an incorruptible Senate stopped the deceased. This Senate was composed of sixteen Priests of the labyrinth, not counting their Chief, and two Judges chosen from each of the twelve ancient Nomes <term>Nomes: The administrative provinces or districts of ancient Egypt.</term>. 

There, after listening to the discourse of the Chief of the Priests who accompanied the deceased King, the Head of the Senate allowed all those present to bring proven accusations against the dead man. The resulting sentence either allowed him to be admitted into the boat by the ferryman, whom they called Charon in their language, or deprived him of burial. This judgment was carried out by ballot, that is to say, by slips of paper that the Judges dropped into that terrible urn—the mere thought of which kept the ancient Kings steadfast in the practice of justice.

Furthermore, into whichever tomb the Kings and even private citizens were carried, it was * always necessary to undergo an examination before Judges who were always men of the highest reputation for probity. These judges could only be chosen from among the <term>Initiates: Individuals who had been formally admitted into the secret religious mysteries and knowledge of the Egyptian priesthood.</term>; and the selection was made each time by people drawn from all classes of citizens of a city, if it concerned a private individual, or from the subjects of a Kingdom, if it concerned a Sovereign. The ballots on which the names of the Judges were written were opened and counted in front of everyone. But regarding the Kings who were carried to the labyrinth, all of Egypt, according to the distribution of the twelve ancient <term>Nomes: The administrative provinces or districts of ancient Egypt.</term>, participated in the choice of the Judges. Moreover, it was only at the labyrinth that they performed that great number of other ceremonies, from which the poet Orpheus—whom we shall soon see in Egypt, and who witnessed them on the occasion of another King—derived the greatest part of the description of the underworld as he gave it in his verses; and as it was followed by Homer among the Greeks, and by Virgil among the Latins. <note>The author suggests that the classical Greek and Roman visions of the afterlife—Hades and the Elysian Fields—were actually poetic adaptations of real Egyptian funerary rituals witnessed by early travelers.</note>

The fortieth day since the death of the Queen having arrived, everyone was prepared for the departure of the convoy. The forty leagues of distance from Memphis to the labyrinth were to be covered in a march of ten days and ten nights, counting the pauses which were all strictly regulated. They had placed under the vestibule of the palace—which was closed to the daylight and illuminated by lamps—a great four-wheeled chariot entirely covered in gold. Furthermore, the entire machine was suspended between its carrying-poles in such a way that it could never lose its level; and moreover, the roads—which were already very fine in Egypt—had been specially prepared for this journey. In short, this chariot seems to have served as a model for the one in which the body of the deceased **Alexander** was later transported from **Babylon** to **Alexandria**.

One could not express the profusion of wines and meats consumed on this occasion; and nothing better conveyed the abundance of Egypt and the wealth of the Egyptians. As she could not raise him to the height she desired except at the expense of the young Sethos <note>Sethos is the King's son from his first marriage and the rightful heir.</note>, she realized that she would have difficulty carrying out the injustices, and perhaps the crimes, which she foresaw would be necessary, so long as there reigned at Court and among the principal members of the State a certain spirit of equity, reason, and order which had been established there under several previous Kings. Thus, she formed a plan to first corrupt the Court; rightly hoping that a corrupted Court would soon provide her for high positions either with vile men who would not contradict her, or with wicked men who would assist her. 

But, in a move that showed her very fine intelligence for evil, she understood that a sufficiently disguised and at the same time very certain means of corrupting the Court in a few years was to introduce there, as much as she could, dissipation <note>In this context, "dissipation" refers to a life of frivolous distraction, amusement, and the wasting of mental energy on trivialities.</note> and levity of mind. She already knew from certain personal experiences that men who are enemies of all focus and all serious occupation, and who are given over solely to their whims and their pleasures—even if they initially possessed that common integrity which costs nothing—have no defense against vices that offer them some utility. But as the research of the Egyptians was not limited to this area, one could see, in cabinets fronted with grilles made of that alloy of gold and silver called *electrum*, samples of all natural productions. Even the simplest items became objects of curiosity because of the classes into which they had been organized. This collection did honor, so to speak, to Nature, through the multitude and variety of her gifts; and her riches, thus gathered under their proper names and the inscriptions that distinguished them, appeared in some way more numerous than in nature itself, where they are usually scattered and unknown. This arrangement included all substances collected on the surface or in the depths of the earth, just as she gives them, or which had undergone no operations other than those intended to clean and purify them. Several cities in **Egypt** have taken their names from the monsters worshipped there. There is a **Crocodilopolis** <note>literally "City of the Crocodile"</note>; the **Hippopotamus** is worshipped at **Papremis**, although that city does not bear its name. The least foolish cities seem to be those that direct their worship toward animals useful to man. <margin>* Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I.</margin> * The **Heracleotes** offer incense to the **Ichneumon** <note>The Egyptian mongoose, famous in antiquity for its perceived enmity with the crocodile.</note>, a species of rat the size of a small dog, which kills the **Crocodile** by leaping into its jaws after coating itself in a thick layer of silt that it allows to dry to serve as armor; it is the only animal, the Ancients said, that creates defensive weapons for itself. All of **Egypt** revered the **Ibis**, a species of stork that delivers their cities from the little winged serpents <note>Ancient historians like Herodotus claimed that winged serpents flew from Arabia into Egypt each spring and were intercepted and eaten by the Ibis.</note> brought by the wind from **Africa**; yet the bird itself is very troublesome due to its voracity and its filth. After the elementary propositions which concern only those figures bounded by straight or circular lines, there followed all the branches of Geometry that require no other assistance. Upon this foundation alone had been raised all the Mathematics employed for the needs of men, for the convenience of cities, and for the embellishment of all Egypt; in a word, all practical Geometry. The principles of this Geometry, all written upon columns—though they were not all copied from those of <term>Mercury</term> <note>Referring to the Egyptian god Thoth, whom the Greeks identified with Hermes/Mercury and credited as the inventor of writing and science.</note>, and the dates of most showed they had been discovered since—filled an entire side of this great hall. These discoveries, attributed to the Priests alone since they formed a particular society in Egypt, were no longer on columns; instead, they had been engraved with the appropriate figures upon white marble tablets, higher and wider than the columns. The established theorems and the solved problems were stated there, like those of simple Geometry, without any demonstration. *

The climate of Egypt was found to be favorable for astronomical observations, not only because of the consistently serene sky it enjoys, but also because, being near the Equator, it reveals almost the entire sky, which makes almost direct <term>revolutions</term> <note>Original: "revolutions presque droites." It is by this advantage of location that the shepherds, who spent their nights in the open countryside, had been the first astronomers; especially as it was impossible for them not to notice the different heights of the constellations at different hours of the night, the successive rising of those that emerge from the sun's rays during the course of the year, and the particular path of the planets, which is usually contrary to the daily movement of the entire sky.

The Egyptians justly boasted of having provided Solon and Lycurgus <note>Solon was the famous lawmaker of Athens, and Lycurgus the legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note> with the finest laws, which these two Greeks brought back from Egypt, one to Athens and the other to Sparta. * One of the most remarkable is that which ordered every common man in Egypt to declare to the Judges each year how he intended to earn his living; and he was forbidden during that time, at least, to do any other thing under penalty of death. In this way, everyone worked with all their might. This activity, which still reigns in our city of Alexandria, caused the Emperor Hadrian <note>Roman Emperor from 117 to 138 CE.</note> † to say that there is no man in this great city who is not assigned a profession or a trade. Even the blind, he adds, have their work. Even those with gout <note>A painful form of arthritis; here used to show that even the infirm contributed.</note> are not inactive, if they have only their hands or their feet free. This is but one example of an infinite number of excellent laws which spread from Egypt to the wisest of Peoples, and some of which are even recognizable in Roman Law ‡.

The Kings of Egypt had always favored these Academies <note>Institutions of higher learning and research.</note>, persuaded as they were that the love of the Sciences and the rest they demand keeps all thoughts of revolt and sedition away from men's minds. Besides the fact that the Sciences exercise and adorn the mind, they also give it a certain solidity and a certain uprightness which usually prevents men not only from being frivolous, but also from being wicked. 

Various Princes had experienced this through the great Ministers, the great Magistrates, and even the great Captains <note>Military leaders.</note> that these Schools had provided them. For to say everything here that belongs to this subject, physical exercises succeeded those of the mind. I am not speaking only of wrestling, swimming, running on foot or on horseback, climbing a simple rope to high summits, and walking there to steady one's eyes and steps—all things important to war, whether for battles or for sieges—I also mean all the parts of the military art that demand study and knowledge. 

One saw the young Lords <note>Nobles or young men of high birth.</note> competing with one another to take the distances of inaccessible places and the measurements of every kind of Fortification. They attentively followed famous Architects in the execution of their immense undertakings, in order to learn from them the proportions of the foundations of walls in relation to their heights; the supports and the span of those vaults as solid as they were light, and the difference of the woods used

The primary motive for this institution <note>The practice of having priests present at court.</note> had been to preserve Religion in the souls of Kings and decency in Courts where, contrary to the custom of other nations, women were always with the men. The Priests themselves had profited from this advantage, adopting the manners of high society in exchange for the knowledge they brought there. Together, they finally formed that assembly—perhaps the only one deserving to be called **good company**—that is to say, people of high rank mixed with people of wit and learning. Thus, no rules were imposed upon the conversations, but they were held by well-regulated minds: and as each person spoke only according to the measure of their genius and knowledge, all the people of the Court, though in different degrees of enlightenment, made themselves almost equally estimable. They even held it as a maxim <note>A fundamental rule or principle of conduct.</note> that wit <term>bel esprit: a 17th and 18th-century term for clever, sparkling intelligence often associated with quick conversation rather than deep study</term> is not the greatest quality a man can possess—not only in relation to affairs of State and war, which are entrusted more often to sensible and experienced men than to wits; but even in relation to the conduct of life and the pleasures of society.

<margin><image-desc>A horizontal pencil mark in the right margin next to line 26.</image-desc></margin>This solidity of mind <note>Intellectual depth and stability.</note> which appeared in the occupations and even the conversations of the Egyptians extended even to matters of pure pleasure. In this way, they protected themselves from a public evil that has always reigned among the Greeks: that if there are writers of ill-repute in their personal lives, it is they who take it upon themselves to correct the human race through Satires <note>Literary works that use humor, irony, or exaggeration to expose and criticize people's stupidity or vices.</note>, which almost never attack anyone but people of merit, whom a just reputation has placed above them. At the entrance of one of these galleries, one found to the right and left columns of wood or stone, crudely carved, roughly the height and thickness of a man. The name of the God and the Hero one had wished to represent was written on some of them; and that was all the Sculpture of the earliest times. Moving forward, one saw the human form develop more and more: But the two legs were still joined together, and the two arms pressed to the body along their length. The hall of instruments was also the treasury of the antiquities of this art. One learned there that the **reed-pipe** <note>The original term is *chalumeau*, a rustic reed instrument and ancestor of the modern clarinet.</note>, the **pastoral flute**, and other **wind instruments** were the first to be invented. One could even see there the multi-piped flute of unequal lengths <note>Commonly known as Panpipes or the *syrinx*.</note>, which was used before **Osiris** <note>The major Egyptian deity, here credited as a civilizing hero and inventor.</note> invented the simple flute, which alone can produce all the tones of the former. This Hero used it to accompany the hymns he sang in honor of the Gods; and also the verses which, according to **Plutarch** <note>A Greek-Roman historian and philosopher (c. 46 – 120 AD) who wrote extensively on Egyptian mythology.</note>, contained the moral precepts he gave to the people he had assembled, and whose manners he wished to soften. <margin>3</margin> The same Osiris later invented the **trumpet** and the **kettledrums** to stir the spirits of the soldiers he employed in his conquests. Afterwards, **Mercury** <note>The Roman name for the god Hermes, often identified by the Greeks with the Egyptian god Thoth, the patron of writing and wisdom.</note> discovered the **lyre**, which allows the musician the freedom to join his voice and words to the sounds of his instrument. In some ancient monuments, this God is seen with lyres of seven strings, of which it is claimed that the two outer strings, when struck together, formed the <term>diapason</term> <note>From the Greek *dia pason*, meaning "through all [the notes]"; it refers here to the interval of an octave.</note> or the octave, even before the penultimate string—which makes the scale complete—had been introduced into the <term>diatonic system</term>. After the lyres, the hall at **Memphis** <note>A capital of ancient Egypt, depicted here as a center of learning and preservation.</note> displayed the first soundboards or bodies of instruments; these are so effective for strengthening sounds that are otherwise too weak when held only within a single frame of unyielding wood, such as that which supports the strings of a lyre. The Egyptians invited young men and young girls to learn and even to perform all genres of Music, to make themselves more polite and more agreeable: and it is by their example that the Greeks placed Music among the disciplines that enter into the instruction of youth.

One sees by this slight sketch that however beautiful private educations may be, they will never have the advantages of this public education of the Egyptians. But what I value most about it is that it did not abandon young people as modern educations do, upon leaving childhood; that is to say, at the time when their more formed minds are capable of knowledge either deeper in itself, or more important for the fatherland; and when, moreover, they need to be defended against the first passions of youth. Because of this, that Court, which was formerly the center of good taste for all kinds of subjects and the model of the purity of the Egyptian language <note>While the setting is ancient Egypt, the author is critiquing the 18th-century French linguistic debates and the role of the "salons" in shaping the language.</note>, was no longer anything but the residence of ignorance or indifference toward everything that can serve as an object for the mind and reason. But the <term>modern wits</term> <note>original: "beaux eſprits"; here used disparagingly to describe socialites who prioritize cleverness over genuine knowledge.</note>, forgetting that language can never be anything but the work of the Public, wanted to introduce, by their own private authority, an infinity of bizarre turns of phrase and terms; which, far from being adopted by common usage, were avoided with extreme care by all those who wished to preserve some dignity in their writings.

The Queen, who watched this progress closely, was already reaping the fruit of her enterprise through the contempt, hatred, and jealousy that animated the courtiers against one another. Men and women alike, they had all arrived—through dissipation and lightheadedness, just as the Queen had foreseen—at the total loss of <term>morals</term> <note>original: "moeurs"; refers to the customs, habits, and moral character of a society.</note>. The entire Pyramid is formed by courses <note>In masonry, a "course" (French: *assise*) is a continuous layer of stones of the same height.</note> that gradually narrow until the final one, which leaves a platform at the summit where each of the four sides is no more than twelve feet wide. The edges of these courses, whose height also decreases as they rise, serve as steps to reach the top. Among all those who often accompanied Sethos and Amedès on this walk, only the boldest undertook the climb to reach the platform; and there was no one who descended in any way other than by turning their back to the countryside, in order to use their hands for support, and especially for fear that vertigo <note>original: *l’égarement de la vûë*, literally "the straying of the sight," referring to the dizziness caused by looking down from a great height</note> might cause a misstep.

Sethos, who had already undergone several very hazardous exercises, did not understand why Amedès would not permit him to undertake this one, which caused him no fear. Amedès finally said to him: "Prince, the interest I take in your life and your honor forbids me from exposing you to this trial, until you are in a condition to descend the Pyramid with your face turned toward the countryside. It is not fitting for a Prince such as you to show the slightest sign of fear on any occasion whatever." 

Hardly had Amedès finished these words than Sethos, running to the Pyramid and placing both hands on the first courses, which are four feet high, raised himself with marvelous lightness and grace onto each one; until, reaching those which were only a foot high, he climbed them like ordinary stairs, and in a short time found himself atop the platform. There he

->### S E T H O S,<-

Access would not have been permitted to the <term>uninitiated</term> <note>original: *profanes*. In this context, it refers to those who have not yet been admitted to the sacred religious mysteries of Egypt.</note>—such as Sethos still was—if the King who had it built had been buried there. But as an empty tomb, it was left to be explored by those who had the patience and the courage. Since it involved traversing dark and deep places, Amedès was convinced that this trial was excellent against the <term>panic terrors</term> <note>A historical term for sudden, overwhelming fear, often attributed by the ancients to the god Pan.</note> that seize most people in the darkness, and against the fear of ghosts with which popular rumor filled uninhabited buildings then as it does now. But this prospect was nothing yet in comparison to a far greater design that he conceived on this occasion, which was to be the crowning achievement of Sethos's education.

   It was for this reason that Amedès said to him while leading him back alone one evening: "Prince, the visit to the interior of the Pyramid, in the manner that it is important for you to do it, is an undertaking entirely different from what you have in mind. Its secret paths lead men cherished by the Gods to a destination <note>original: *terme*, implying a final goal or a stage of completion.</note> that I cannot even name for you, and for which the Gods must create the desire within you. The entrance to the Pyramid is open to everyone; but I pity those who, exiting through the same door by which they entered, have satisfied only a very imperfect curiosity, and have seen only what they are permitted to recount."

A discourse so new to the young Prince cast into his soul an impatience that went so far as to make him take the resolution to clear up this enigma immediately, even by deceiving the vigilance of his Governor if he refused to accompany him. Amedès

<header>B O O K II.</header>

Amedès, who read this thought in his eyes, did not give him time to respond, and said to him: "My Lord, I will lead you myself to this undertaking, which is nearly impossible to begin alone, though it must be finished alone. But I am not permitted to expose you to the dangers encountered there until the opportunities that may present themselves in time have sufficiently assured me of your courage, and above all, of your **prudence** <note>In 18th-century literature, "prudence" (original: *prudence*) refers to the classical virtue of practical wisdom and the ability to keep one's counsel, which was essential for the religious initiations described in this novel.</note>. I have cause to be satisfied with the signs I have seen of them until now. The age you are entering will demand greater ones and will undoubtedly soon provide you with the means to demonstrate them. Therefore, do not listen to your impatience, but rely upon mine; begin, however, by keeping the secret of the little I have just told you, so that you may accustom yourself to keeping greater ones."

The young Prince, who could not yet fix his mind upon the meaning of these words, said to Amedès: that without wishing to penetrate further into the mystery at hand, the first mark of the **prudence** that his Master wished to see in him was to trust himself entirely to his guidance.

# SETHOS.

## BOOK THREE.

**T**he war with which the King of Memphis <note>In the context of this 18th-century novel, Memphis represents the seat of the Egyptian monarchy where the protagonist is being raised.</note> was threatened, especially from the direction of Thebes, caused Sethos a kind of joy; because he judged that war alone could provide him the means to provide the proof that Amedès expected of him. This wise Governor, who had noticed it, said to him one day: "Although in the undertaking of which I spoke to you on the occasion of the Pyramid, it is not a matter of performing sudden strikes <term>sudden strikes: (original: *coups de main*) military maneuvers involving surprise and speed to seize a position</term>, nor of fighting armed enemies, I cannot sufficiently praise the goodness within the vague sentiment that draws you toward war. But," he added, "I would not be fulfilling the function I have the honor of exercising for a Prince born for the Throne, if I did not warn him that a King who loves his people always regards war as a misfortune, and makes every effort to prevent it so long as they do not detract from his well-established rights or his well-understood honor. This maxim, deeply engraved in the heart of a King, becomes the very principle of true bravery, which is all the more ardent..."

All these young men were delighted by the opportunity Amedès presented, and they promised to follow his orders faithfully in carrying out this plan. He replied that Prince *Sethos*—whom he would nevertheless keep a close watch over—should be their leader in this expedition. By commanding them, the Prince would learn to make good use not only of the strength of his officers' arms, but also of their counsel; and thus, as in a well-organized army and a well-conducted war, they would all share in the glory of success—not only in proportion to their courage, but also in proportion to their intelligence.

He ordered others to notice the thickness of the Serpent by a similar comparison with the height of the objects near which it would pass; and he charged himself, along with the last group—among whom was Amedès <note>Amedès is Sethos's tutor and loyal companion, who often provides guidance and moral support.</note>—to follow the route of the animal with their eyes, and even to advance enough to discover, if possible, the entrance to its cave. Amedès showed, by his particular obedience, the approval he gave to his pupil.

What Sethos had foreseen did not fail to happen. From as far away as the Serpent perceived this troop of people on horseback, composed with the Slaves of about twenty persons, it began to unroll itself. Once the assessment was complete, they found it was approximately forty-five feet <note>The 18th-century French "foot" (pied du roi) was slightly larger than the modern English foot, making this creature nearly 15 meters long.</note> long, and about six feet in diameter—or eighteen to nineteen feet in circumference—at the thickest part of its body, which was its head.

While most of the young hunters worked on this estimation, Sethos, Amedès, and three or four others followed the monster from a distance. They concealed themselves as much as they could from its sight, either by taking detours or by using the most covered paths the nature of the terrain could offer, for fear that it might hide its retreat, as many animals do when they believe they are being watched.

The creature turned around the base that supports the first peak of the mountain, until it reached the spot almost opposite to the one facing the marsh from which it had come. Our observers had the pleasure of seeing it enter through an opening which it filled almost entirely.

### B O O K III.

"Because I attempted a reckless undertaking, the just and merciful Gods hold me forever in a favorable prison; fear and love the Gods." This formula caused them to be regarded as dead, and released their families from any further obligation toward them. They were certain, in fact, never to speak of their lives to any profane person <note>In the context of ancient mysteries, a "profane" person refers to the uninitiated public who were not permitted to know the sacred secrets.</note>. The other Officers of the second rank, even the children of those men, had the freedom—not to change their status, which was forbidden to any Egyptian—but to serve in their turn in the superior Temples, and even to speak to everyone just as the Priests did. This was because they were bound to secrecy by an oath that the Priests did not even deign to require from those who, having succumbed during their trials, were said to have "failed their word to themselves."

These allegories themselves are of little consequence in comparison to the mysteries of Ceres <note>Also known as the Eleusinian Mysteries, the most famous of the secret religious rites of ancient Greece.</note> which he actually established at Eleusis on the model of those of Isis; and which he divided into the "great" and "small" mysteries, with the same intent as the distinction made in Egypt between the Great and the Small Initiation. The former was given only to the natives of the country, and foreigners were granted only the latter. Both groups, at Eleusis as in Egypt, were bound to a secret that had never been violated without costing the culprit his life—either through a regular legal sentence or by other means, in whatever part of the world he might be—and they never failed to change, at least in part, the revealed practice. This is why we know so little about these ancient ceremonies. The little that I know myself has only reached me...

Although there are still Initiations today in both Egypt and Greece, they are no longer so harsh; and the mysteries to which they lead are no longer so secret. Persons of great distinction are received there without trial. Even children are quite often consecrated, without condition and by the sole devotion of their parents, to either Isis or Ceres <note>In ancient syncretism, the Egyptian goddess Isis was frequently identified with the Greek goddess Ceres (Demeter), as both were associated with fertility, agriculture, and the mysteries of life and death.</note>, who are fundamentally the same Goddess.

In the morning session, one of them spent an hour explaining the general principles of the Egyptian Religion. He <margin>*</margin> established the concept of a single God who had conceived the world through his intelligence before forming it by his will <note>This philosophical view reflects the 18th-century "Prisca Theologia," the belief that ancient civilizations held a pure monotheistic truth before it was corrupted into polytheism.</note>. However, to accommodate human weakness, they were permitted to worship the different attributes of his essence and the various effects of his goodness under the symbols of the Heavenly Bodies, such as the Sun and the Planets; great personages such as Osiris, Jupiter, and Mercury <note>The author uses Roman names for Egyptian deities, following the tradition of "Interpretatio Romana." Mercury likely refers to Thoth, and Jupiter to Amun.</note>; and even terrestrial bodies such as animals and plants <margin>†</margin>. He added that the subordinate Gods were also the spirits whom the supreme God saw fit to employ as ministers in the Government of the Universe. He did not forget the spirit that tempts men and disrupts nature, represented by Typhon <note>Typhon was the Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, associated with chaos and storms.</note>, by evil spirits, and by noxious animals or venomous plants. Egyptians, through this complex <note>The original French uses "confuse," which in this 18th-century context implies "fused together" or "intricate" rather than "muddled."</note> idea of the unity of the Divine Being and the multiplicity of its symbols, were the first authors of what was most sublime in Philosophical opinions and most coarse in popular superstitions. Furthermore, the physical and historical origins of the names of these secondary Gods and the varieties of their worship were presented in such a learned and curious manner that Sethos sometimes felt envy toward these men who, being delivered from all the burdens of life, could devote themselves entirely to such satisfying research.

The evening conference lasted an hour and a half. It dealt only with <term>morality</term> <note>In this 18th-century context, "morality" (morale) refers to ethics and the practical application of virtue to one's specific social station.</note>. Beyond this, all the Priests assigned to sacred instruction were required to receive him in their private studies at whatever hour he might present himself during the intervals between his exercises. ### BOOK III.

what the <term>Initiate</term> <note>A person who has been formally admitted into the sacred mysteries of Egypt through specific rituals and trials.</note> is, holds, so to speak, his life in his hand; and he only continues to use it because his duty has not yet demanded it of him. Glory is usually attached to the great virtues seen practiced by the Initiates; but it is neither their motive nor their goal. It is important to preserve the idea and the name of glory among men, especially regarding those who, being born in a high degree of elevation <note>Refers to those born into the nobility or high social classes.</note>, cannot usually be animated by any other perceptible interest. But at heart, glory is the spur only for the weak or the beginners. The motive of the Initiate is the voice of his duty; and his goal is its fulfillment. It is for this reason, he said, that we see many among our Initiates who have preferred to render obscure and hidden services to their Prince or their Country <note>original: "Patrie"; signifies the ancestral homeland or nation-state.</note>, rather than being clothed in the most brilliant dignities. He bears witness to the uprightness of his own intentions, but he distrusts his own thoughts and views. He does not feel capable of committing injustices or crimes, but he recognizes in himself all the weaknesses of nature. Always on guard against faults, he is always ready to admit that he has committed them. He is, finally, a man without flaw who is always working to correct himself, and a perfect man who is always striving to perfect himself.

But, my father," he continued, "I have been quite blind not to have perceived in you yourself these sublime virtues of which they have painted such a rich picture for me. My son," Amedès said to him, "it is a great deal for me if it is true that I have not dishonored the title of Initiate that I bear. But it is another than I who must give it its luster. The greatness of your birth imposes more extensive laws upon you, and also gives you greater facilities than I have for the practice—

He judged by this that the Priests regarded the accuracy of his answers as a very important matter, and that he should reflect upon them very deeply. There is no stronger drive among men than that of upholding the honor of an exclusive group, into which one is admitted on the basis of merit and virtue. This drive was perhaps less effective among foreign Initiates because, losing sight of the example of their fellows, they might forget their commitments. But having received only the second Initiation, or the private Initiation, they were not entirely of the same rank as the **Egyptian** Initiates; and the honor of the order did not depend on them.

## *BOOK FOUR.*

About twenty years had then passed since a **Tyrian** <note>A person from Tyre, a major Phoenician city-state in modern-day Lebanon.</note> named **Zoros**, a descendant of **Cadmus** <note>The legendary Phoenician prince who founded Thebes in Greece and is credited with introducing the alphabet to the Greeks.</note> and a man of courage and intelligence, had founded the city of **Carthage**, or at least had extended the walls of **Carthada**, which was already built. He finally resolved to settle in Carthada himself and to enlarge it. With this design, he brought all his ships there, laden with great riches. He was received with joy by peoples who were not yet in the state of <term>opulence: great wealth or luxurious abundance</term> which they soon achieved through his efforts. He increased and beautified their city to the point of making it unrecognizable; and he left it its ancient name, to which he merely gave a **Phoenician** termination. was valor. Valor itself is rather a natural and advantageous disposition of the soul and the body, than it is a true virtue. One can make of it—as with several other similar qualities—either a good or a bad use. It is found in wicked men; and it has sometimes even made wicked those men who would have been good without it <note>Sethos argues that physical bravery without moral guidance can lead to arrogance or cruelty.</note>. Valor only becomes praiseworthy and respectable through a superior virtue that employs and directs it. This virtue, in the subject or in the citizen, is the love of one's Prince and one's Homeland <note>original: "Patrie"</note> guided by simple obedience. In the Prince or the Head of the Republic <note>In this 18th-century context, "Republic" refers generally to the State or the "commonwealth," whether a monarchy or a democracy.</note>, it is the love of his People, enlightened by the justice he observes even toward his neighbors and his enemies. In the Hero finally, it is the love of mankind in general, or humanity <term>humanité: In the Enlightenment sense, this refers to a philanthropic benevolence and a sense of belonging to the global human family.</term> guided by a zeal founded on a lively hope for the protection of the Gods.

Thus, it is this courageous humanity, this zealous love for the human race, which is the primary virtue of the Hero. True courage—which, generally considered, suits every condition and even every sex, but which, when applied to the exploits of war, is called valor—always consists in braving all sorts of perils to follow duty. It is this sole view of duty that distinguishes true or virtuous valor from blind fury or unjust violence, and which always makes even Heroism reasonable. But I have been taught that there are two kinds of duties: one of state, and the other of inspiration. # S E T H O S, #

to fulfill the ordinary obligations of their status, which are preferable for most men to all others. The duty of inspiration <note>Sethos refers here to a divine or internal "calling" that drives a hero beyond the standard rules of society.</note> belongs only to those whom the Gods seem to draw from the common order to lead them to works more sublime in themselves, and more useful either to their Homeland <note>original: "Patrie"</note> or to the human race: and this latter duty, usually indicated by the singular circumstances in which Providence places certain men, becomes the duty of the Hero. To fulfill it, he needs a valor far elevated above that of common Conquerors; and we also see that true Heroes, or the benefactors of the human race, have always been considered the most courageous of all men. A heart filled with such inspiration—a man touched by true Heroism—runs no risk of stopping in his course; it is only dangerous for him to cross the boundaries of duty. Thus, all his attention is focused on resisting every impulse of valor, or even of an excessive generosity—that is to say, one which would turn only to his own glory, without contributing to the good of the men to whom he has consecrated his labors and his life. He knows that sublime virtue is recognized, not by superfluous works, but by the entire and perfect fulfillment of those which are imposed upon him. His duty is as extensive as the public utility <term>utilité publique: A central Enlightenment concept where the morality of an action is judged by its benefit to the community at large.</term>; but public utility also marks the boundaries that he never wishes to cross. In effect, the Hero, far from seeking a vain glory, exposes himself for the service of his Homeland or the human race to the bizarre interpretations or the unjust condemnations of the very men he wishes to serve.

### BOOK IV.

The next day, at the break of dawn, the **Chief Priest of Expiations**, followed by several officers of the second Order, went to find the Carthaginian in his prison. It had a door opening onto the bank of the **subterranean canal** <note>A man-made underground waterway used in the fictional "Egyptian mysteries" to simulate terrifying trials by water.</note> that was crossed during the trials of **Initiation**. This door was near the waterfall, though on this side of the bars through which the water entered the canal. It was opened for him from the inside, and he was led out that way. Both banks were lit by several torches, and he saw a terrible display of machines and people appointed to operate them. 

On the bank on his side was a bronze vat filled with a somewhat thick liquid, and right next to the water, a piece of iron, glowing red-hot, the length of the tallest man and curved across its width by about three feet; so that it resembled a long and wide pipe cut in half along its length. It was currently supported by iron feet over a burning brazier. One of its ends tilted slightly toward the water. An officer of the second Order held in his hands the end of a rope the thickness of a little finger, which, crossing the entire width of the canal, wound around the concave circumference of a very large wheel placed on the opposite shore. 

This wheel was traversed at its center by an axle, to which were attached two strong cranks that other men were preparing to turn when the time came. Several priests, some initiates, **Sethos**, and **Orpheus** <note>The legendary Greek poet and musician, who in this narrative is depicted as an initiate of the Egyptian mysteries, highlighting the idea that Greek culture was a "daughter" of Egyptian wisdom.</note> were seated to the right and left beside the wheel. Those who held the Patient submerged in the vat took care to change their hand positions, so that there was not a single spot on the body that was not anointed with the liquid. From the dawn of the third day, the preparations for the **expiatory sacrifice** <term>Sacrifice expiatoire: a ritual offering intended to make amends for a sin or crime</term> began. I shall not provide the full details of a ceremony that occupied nearly the entire day. I will say only that it consisted of two main parts, both conducted within the Temple, though the first was held behind closed doors. This first part was focused on appeasing **Typhon**, the malevolent spirit or God whom the Egyptians regarded as the instigator of all human crimes and the author of all their misfortunes. It is from this concept that **Zoroaster** and the Magi of Persia derived their evil spirit **Ahriman** <note>original: "Arimane"</note>, who is always opposed to **Ohrmazd** <note>original: "Orimase"</note>, the universal benefactor; from it, the Greeks derived their **Apopompaioi** <note>original: "Apopompées"; deities who ward off evil</note> or **Apotropaioi** <note>original: "Apotropées"</note> gods, who were opposed to **Olympian Jupiter**; and the Latins their **Averrunci** <note>original: "Averrunques"; deities who avert misfortune</note> gods, opposed to **Helpful Jupiter** <note>original: "*Jovi juvanti*"</note>. 

In Egypt, on this occasion, a **red ox** was brought into the rear of the sanctuary, as it was supposed that Typhon had been of that color <note>Ancient Egyptian tradition associated red-haired animals and people with Set, whom the Greeks identified as Typhon</note>. The High Priest of Atonements laid his hand upon the victim's head and pronounced these words, a portion of which is recorded by **Herodotus** <margin>Book 2.</margin>:

> May the crime of the guilty person here present, and all the unfortunate consequences it should bring upon him, his family, and his country, pass onto this animal that we sacrifice to you, O Typhon, to represent through its death the death of the man who is the object of your hatred.

<insert>
Immediately, the ox was struck between the horns and fell to the ground. After slitting its throat, the Priest sprinkled its blood upon the guilty man, who was still clothed in his sackcloth. However, unlike other **sacrifices**, where the Priests and even those who had made the offering carried away the pieces of the victim to share and eat them, all parts of the **expiatory victim** <term>expiatory victim: an animal sacrificed specifically to atone for a crime or sin, rather than for a celebratory meal</term> were thrown out into the fields.
</insert>

Efforts were then made to appease the **manes** <term>manes: the spirits or souls of the deceased, whom the living sought to keep at peace</term> of the dead. Those who came to be purified found merchants around the Temple who sold them crudely made figures of men and women, always set upon a small pedestal. These were made of gold, silver, or bronze, and their height ranged from three to twelve inches. They were intended to represent, interchangeably within the ceremony, either the person or sometimes even the Divinity who had been offended. The sellers advised the **Postulants** <term>Postulants: candidates or petitioners seeking ritual cleansing</term> for expiation to take one of a material and height proportionate to their means. **Saphon** <note>Saphon is a character in this narrative seeking atonement for the death of Giscon</note>, before entering, had not failed to choose a gold one from among the tallest; and he was to leave it in the Temple as a fee, according to custom. The Priest, having placed it before him on a table to represent **Giscon**, delivered a eulogy for him as if on behalf of the guilty man, who was always expected to acknowledge the good qualities of the man he had killed. In this eulogy—prepared the previous day and recorded immediately in the **Book of Ceremonials**—the Priest read several specific details of the life of the deceased, which he could have known only from the deposition of the guilty man, and which often surprised the Priest greatly.

...to reveal the things I have learned, and to bring to light what took place in the bowels of the earth and under the impenetrable veil of the deepest silence. Scarcely had **Sethos** descended into the subterranean passage from the side of the upper **Temple**, when he was extremely surprised to hear the cries of children. **Orpheus**, who had been as surprised as he was, later supposed that children who died while still nursing were placed at the entrance to the **Underworld** <note>The author suggests that the Greek poet Orpheus based his description of Hades on these real Egyptian rituals he witnessed during his own initiation.</note>. These were the children of the **Priests**, whose mothers always went to give birth in quarters prepared for them there. The reason for this practice was to accustom the temperament of these children, from the very first moment of their birth, to these subterranean dwellings in which they were to spend a large part of their lives. Furthermore, they did not want any kind of noise or distraction, nor even any fatherly weakness, to divert the **Priests** from their meditations and studies; and they were made, from then on, to view their children as belonging to the <term>Sacerdotal College</term> <note>The organized body or "college" of priests who lived and worked together.</note> and not to themselves. It is from here that **Lycurgus** <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note> had taken the model and the motive for the public education of the **Spartans**. The **Egyptian Priestesses** nursed their children themselves if their health permitted; otherwise, the wives of the **Officers of the second Order** served as their wet-nurses. The new **Initiate** saw these quarters only from the doorway and for only a moment. Only the **Priest-Physicians** were permitted to enter, and they regulated all the internal discipline <note>original: "police"</note>. The new **Initiate** would spend, for the first time, a quarter of an hour in each of these Schools. They were always very full, because they existed only in the twelve ancient **Temples**, and the Priests of the dependent towns were obliged to send their children to the principal Temple to receive a uniform education. However, one should not believe that they were all sent back to the city they came from, just as all children born in **Memphis** did not necessarily find their permanent placement there. This subterranean city, which filled two-thirds of the total square area, had several streets of varying sizes, and even squares all equally illuminated by lamps. Since the initial construction of these dwellings, people had even thought to pierce through the earth covering them in several places all the way to the top; not truly to bring in daylight, which would never have been sufficient, but to provide healthy air for the habitations the Priests had established, and which the original builders had not considered. 

These openings, which all corresponded to the squares of the underground level, ended above in the form of wells that opened into the courtyards or gardens of the **Sacerdotal Houses** <note>Priestly residences or community buildings.</note>, many of which had been built specifically for this purpose. But more serious faults brought upon them truly painful punishments. Although the **Priests** and **Priestesses** were subject to certain kinds of punishments, these were strictly hidden, either from the **Initiates** to preserve the honor of the **Priesthood** <note>original: "Sacerdoce."</note>, or from the **Second Officers** to maintain the respect they owed their masters. This precaution was only set aside for scandalous faults that had disturbed the order of the house or had become known to the public. For such offenses, they were condemned to one or several years of silence, which they spent in the underground chambers. Sethos saw some Priests and Priestesses dressed in black and deprived of their priestly tunics, walking around the Field of Tears while hiding their faces, or returning to the adjacent prison. There, each had their own cell, and they found no conversation except with the books that were not denied to them. the middle of the entire grounds, large spaces had been preserved that served as an **arena** or **circus** <note>In the Roman sense: an oval track or ring for physical competition.</note> for various physical exercises. There, they accustomed not only their subordinate officers—who required great dexterity in many of their duties—but also the children of the Priests, both boys and girls, according to what was appropriate for their sex. Their primary goal was to make their bodies supple and to form their physical carriage in general, as was done for other Egyptians. The result of this attention was to attract a very great number of people to the Temples, drawn by the precision and nobility with which they performed the numerous ceremonies of Religion. And in the social interactions of life, although the Priests and Priestesses displayed more restraint and modesty in their bearing than people of the world, one noticed in their countenance and their actions a grace and facility that connoisseurs often held up as a model.

But they had a reason far more important to them for making their children skilled in all the components that have since comprised, among the Greeks and Romans, the **Art of Serious Representations** <note>The author refers here to the art of theater and dramatic performance.</note>. It was through theatrical scenes that the Priests of the principal Temples of Egypt, and especially those of **Heliopolis** and **Memphis**, responded to consultations made to them regarding future or hidden things *. It must also be admitted that as they did not have to deal with an entire amphitheater full of people, they placed the single person, or at least the few people to whom they had to respond each time, in the specific viewpoint that created an invincible illusion for them.

this Inscription, which was copied from the Egyptian onto a marble slab that can still be seen in a Temple at Capua: <note>original Latin: "Te, tibi, una, quæ es omnia, Dea Isis."</note> *To you, for you, the one who is all, Goddess Isis.* That is to say: We offer this to you, unique and universal Divinity, Goddess Isis. The young women who had brought the offering would withdraw through the back of the Sanctuary; and the Priests would enter to complete the ceremonies, which lasted nearly two hours, always to the sound of voices and instruments. These ceremonies differed across the four Seasons, as did the Hymns that served as the subjects for the Music; many of these hymns later passed into the Higher Temples and then into the mouths of all Egyptians, owing to the beauty of the Verses and the songs, which sometimes even possessed the charm of novelty.

These were the mysteries of Isis, whose secrecy made them so venerable during the golden ages of Egypt; once revealed through the chaos of wars and the violence of conquerors, they served as a model or a pretext for those dissolute practices that have since flooded the Temples of Greece and Italy. It is established by all the records that have fallen into my hands that the Priests and the Attendees in ancient Egypt never abused the Spectacle that unfolded before their eyes in the **Pantheon** <note>In this context, the central subterranean sanctuary of all the gods.</note>. Orpheus expressed the restraint to which they were bound on this matter by the majesty of the place, using the image of Tantalus in the midst of the waters <note>In Greek mythology, Tantalus was punished with eternal hunger and thirst despite being surrounded by food and water he could not reach; here, the author uses him as a symbol of disciplined restraint in the face of sensory beauty.</note>.

Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta, credited with the city's military-oriented reformation and strict social codes.</note>, taking his thinking further, had imagined that the wisdom prevailing in Egypt across the entire Sacerdotal Order—where no memory existed of any disorder arising from the passion for women—stemmed from the fact that they saw them thus every day in the open. It was this that led him to establish in his Republic those wrestling matches <note>Refers to the Spartan tradition where young men and women exercised together, often minimally clothed or naked, to promote health and social bonding.</note> in which the young people of both sexes practiced naked in the presence of everyone. He used to say that the Lacedaemonian <note>Another name for the Spartans.</note> girls were covered in the arena by public decency, based on what he had heard from the Priests of Egypt: that their own daughters were covered in the Pantheon <note>Used here generally to refer to the temple complex or the collective of Egyptian deities.</note> by religious sanctity. Nevertheless, longer experience has convinced Sages of the truth of this maxim pronounced by the old Latin poet Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239 – 169 BC), often considered the father of Roman poetry.</note>, who said that nakedness exposed to the eyes of Citizens is the primary source of all the disorders of a Republic. *The beginning of vice is to strip bodies bare among citizens.* <note>original: "Flagitii principium est nudare inter cives corpora."</note> Indeed, one needs only a very slight acquaintance with Greek and Roman history to know to what shameful excesses the first communication of the unveiled mysteries of Isis drove these peoples. Even the Egyptians themselves, having fallen from their former severity, had introduced into the Temples they were permitted to build outside of Egypt—and especially in Rome—a corruption so extreme that the Senate issued several decrees to tear down these Temples, which were called Memphitic <note>Pertaining to Memphis, the ancient capital of Egypt; used here to designate Egyptian temples located abroad.</note>. Popular superstition, supported by the deep-rooted habit of debauchery, had rendered these decrees useless, until the Consul Paul <note>Likely referring to Lucius Aemilius Paullus, a Roman consul known for his strict adherence to traditional Roman religious law, who famously took an axe to the temples of Isis when workers refused to do so in 50 BC.</note>

One can see from the description by Apuleius <note>Lucius Apuleius (c. 124 – c. 170 AD), a Roman author whose work *The Golden Ass* provides a famous, though later, account of the procession of Isis.</note> alone that the worldly women initiated into the mysteries of **Isis** after the devastation of Egypt took the place of these girls in such processions, where even the other priestesses did not previously attend. Following these girls came a very large musical choir composed of **Priests** and their children, who announced the **Tabernacle of Isis**. It was carried on the shoulders of eight Priests: but it was immediately preceded by girls of the second order, dressed in very fine white wool and adorned with flowers, who, holding <term>sistrums<gloss>An ancient Egyptian percussion instrument consisting of a metal frame with jingling crossbars, used to repel evil spirits and honor the gods.</gloss></term> and <term>crotala<gloss>Small wooden or metal clappers, similar to castanets, used to provide rhythm for religious dances.</gloss></term> in their hands, performed light dances before the Tabernacle—dances that Greece later imitated to excess in its orgies.

Other girls on both sides burned perfumes, the smoke of which surrounded the Tabernacle in such a way that it seemed to always be encased in a cloud. The **High Priest** walked alone behind the Tabernacle. He was dressed in white beneath his tunic, and over it a purple robe lined with ermine, the train of which was carried by two children of the second order. All the Priests of this Class were dressed in black over and under the white tunic. The elders walked closest to the Tabernacle. Thus, unlike the three first Classes, they were followed by their children, whose two files were closed by the four Prefects of education. The *Isiac pomp* <note>original: "pompe Isiaque"</note> <note>The formal, ceremonial procession dedicated to the goddess Isis.</note> properly so-called ended there. It was performed on other occasions, although it was never so numerous or so magnificent as on this one.

The last part of the Procession, or the triumph of the **Initiate**, took on a military air, even in regards to those who were not men of war; because it was supposed that they defended the Fatherland in their own manner: and moreover, even the **Initiates** were indiscriminately of every profession for the service of the King and the Public. Thus, at the end of the second interval, one saw approaching to the sound of fifes and kettledrums three unfurled Standards. The first bore the Symbol of the Kingdom of **Memphis**, which was the **Apis Bull** <note>The sacred bull of Memphis, seen as an intermediary between humans and the gods.</note>; the second that of **Egypt**, which was a **Sphinx**, and the third that of the whole world, which was a **Serpent**,

#### BOOK IV.

The **Initiates** appeared next: they were few in number in each <term>Nome<gloss>An administrative district or province in ancient Egypt.</gloss></term>; and those who held positions either in the military or in the Provinces did not leave them for this ceremony. However, if there were **Initiates** from another **Nome**, they took their place here according to the rank of their reception; for all the **Initiates** of **Egypt** formed but a single body. They marched one by one in their ordinary habit, that is to say, with a vest of fine linen that reached only to the knees, and which they never removed. Over this vest was the robe of their dignity or function; and beside them, and outside the ranks, were the foreign **Initiates**, if any were currently in **Egypt**; and it was in this manner that **Orpheus** <note>The legendary Greek musician and poet, whom eighteenth-century writers often claimed studied under Egyptian priests.</note> assisted at the triumph of **Sethos**. Following this order, one saw Generals of the Army, and even Princes, who, being less senior in their **Initiation**, yielded precedence to simple Citizens.

The new **Initiate** appeared at last, having at his right the youngest of the **Priests**, and at his left the eldest of the **Initiates**. He was dressed, for this first day only, in a white tunic with a train trailing the length of his body. He wore over it a white baldric bordered with black, from which hung a sword whose hilt was merely of steel; but he had for a belt a sash the color of fire and bordered with gold. He wore a crown of **Myrtle** upon his head; and he held in his hand a large **Palm**, the **Symbol of peace**.

### S E T H O S,

Finally, his head was covered with a white veil that descended over his face and even his chest, through which he could see well enough to guide himself, but which prevented anyone from recognizing him. He was followed by a **Triumphal Chariot** drawn by four horses abreast. Four **Virtues** <note>Allegorical figures representing moral excellence.</note> bore a triumphal crown upon the empty seat; and figures of defeated vices lined the entire circumference of the footboard. This chariot was similar, save for a few symbols, to those that carried the Generals of the Army through the capitals of **Egypt** upon returning from a great victory. But the **Initiate** never mounted his own; this was to show that he did not even aspire to the outward honors that his great deeds might deserve. 

Throughout the ages, the **Initiate** had always been welcomed in this ceremony by the great acclamations of the People. However, the extravagance and injustice of the government of **Daluca** <note>In the context of this novel, Daluca refers to a legendary Queen of Egypt whose reign was marked by shifting fortunes and complex governance.</note> made the hope of some relief even more palpable to all the inhabitants of **Memphis**. The **Initiate** was showered with flowers and drenched with precious essences, which were thrown from windows or passed over the heads of the Guards. No music has ever been as touching as the chorus of blessings bestowed upon him. It was for this reason—though the public display might have been less intense in other times—that the **Initiate** always walked veiled; so that he might attribute nothing of these outbursts of public affection to himself, and that he might understand, on the contrary, that they were due only to the high esteem held for the body <note>original: "un corps." Refers to the collective order or society of Initiates.</note> of which he was a part, whose examples he was thereby obliged to follow and whose glory he was to uphold.

### BOOK IV.

Sethos, after having thus made a grand circuit through the City, arrived in the square where the King's Palace stood. The King, the Queen, and a crowd of Courtiers awaited him upon a long balcony, adorned with superb carpets. Osoroth, who was naturally kind-hearted <note>The text highlights the innate goodness of King Osoroth, contrasting him with the more sinister Queen.</note>, seemed to take part in these celebrations, the noise of which was constantly drawing nearer. Even from as far away as he could perceive the final part of this pompous procession, and especially when he caught sight of the head of the **Initiate** <term>Initiate: One who has successfully passed the secret trials and rituals of the Egyptian mysteries.</term>, which stood at least as high as the tallest of the others; he felt a gentle emotion, of which the Queen—an enemy of all things good—immediately conceived a sharp feeling of jealousy. 

But her vexation increased greatly when the **Initiate** mounted a high platform, erected according to custom in front of the Palace balcony. There, he knelt upon a cushion <note>original: "carreau" — a large, ceremonial square cushion used for kneeling during formal or religious events.</note> and made another deep bow to the King. Rising afterward, he drew his sword, as if to offer it for his service. At this action, which the young Prince performed with nobility and marvelous grace, Osoroth, with tears nearly in his eyes, leaned forward and extended his arms as if to embrace the **Initiate**. He then turned to his right and left, as if to impart to every soul the tender admiration with which he was filled. 

The People, encouraged by this example, then uttered a thousand cries of joy addressed to the King. They told him, "Be our Master, and be so for a long life." At the same time, they cast fixed stares upon the Queen which, however, were only insulting in the secret intent of those looking at her—an intent she discerned perfectly. This woman, who, in order to please the King, was obliged to cover [her feelings] with a forced <note>The original French text breaks mid-word here at "for-", which would complete as "forcée" on the following page.</note> smile—
