From the very next day, Sethos and Amedes presented themselves at the Palace for the King’s rising <note>original: "au lever du Roi." A formal courtly ritual where the monarch’s waking and dressing were attended by high-ranking officials and favorites.</note>. Osoroth, in the presence of several Great Men already admitted to the chamber, received his son with open arms. He thanked Amedes for having secured the advantage of the **Initiation** <term>Initiation: In this context, the successful completion of the secret, sacred, and often dangerous trials of the Egyptian mysteries, which granted the candidate elite status.</term>; and he told the young Prince that the war which the King of Thebes had just declared—jointly with the King of This <note>Also known as Thinis, an ancient city in Upper Egypt.</note>—against the Kingdom of Memphis, would soon give him cause to employ the sword he had offered for his service during the previous evening's ceremony. After a conversation that remained general in nature, the King appearing to wish to be alone, Sethos left the room. He was followed by the Courtiers, who all believed that the atmosphere of the Court was about to change, and that Sethos would have a large share in the distribution of military offices.

# S E T H O S,

...tropics, which enclose its annual path, than in the space extending beyond toward one or the other Pole, where its influence is less dominant. This is why the winds, which are caused by the rarefaction <note>The thinning of air as it warms, a correct early scientific understanding of atmospheric pressure changes.</note> of heated air, are more regular in the **Torrid Zone** <note>The region of the Earth between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn; the equatorial region.</note> than anywhere else. The heat of the days and the coolness of the nights always return in the same way throughout the different months of the year. Regarding the rains—the substance of which is provided by the exhalations and vapors spread through the air—it is the **Sun** itself that causes them to rise abundantly in its perpendicular position, and which simultaneously dissolves them into torrents of water.

It follows that, unlike what occurs in the **Temperate Zones** and the **Frigid Zones**, which have Summer when the **Sun** approaches them and Winter when it moves away, Winter—or the rainy season in each of the two parts of the **Torrid Zone**, at least in **Africa**—is the time of the **Sun’s** most direct passage over them. Now, as the sources of the **Nile** are in the Northern part of this zone, the river's first streams swell when the **Sun** is in the Northern signs <note>The zodiac signs associated with the northern hemisphere's spring and summer, such as Aries through Virgo.</note>, which brings us Summer. The same occurs with all rivers that have their sources in the **Torrid Zone**. However, they are not all laden with a **silt** <note>original: "limon"</note> as beneficial as that of the **Nile** for fertilizing the land. This conversation gradually led our Travelers back as far as **Syene** <note>Modern Aswan, located at the First Cataract of the Nile, which served as the southern frontier of ancient Egypt.</note>.

However, in the **Theban Nome** <note>A 'Nome' was a territorial division or administrative province of ancient Egypt.</note>, they were animated by a spirit of rigor which, in Sethos’s judgment, deprived them not only of much of their grace, but also of their value. While in the Sacerdotal Nome of Memphis, virtue was an exercise for honorable men, in **Thebes** it seemed to him a labor for slaves.

Nevertheless, keeping these reflections to himself, Sethos finally found himself returned via the underground route to the capital. The Priests showed him all the beauties of their house, and reserved for the last their **Observatory**.

The apartment bearing this name was situated atop the **Temple of Theban Jupiter** <note>The Greek and Roman name for the Egyptian god Amun, specifically the form worshipped at Thebes (Karnak/Luxor).</note>, and was composed of two long galleries, one above the other. "I believe," he continued, "that if one were to ask a casual observer what size the **Sun** appears to him to be, he would give it about one foot in diameter; because, in fact, if it appears to be a little more than a foot at the **horizon**, it also appears to be a little less at **Noon** <note>original: "le Midi," referring here to the sun's highest point in the sky at midday.</note>. Now, **Astronomers** have found that the diameter of the **Sun's** disk occupies approximately half a **degree** of the sky. Thus, on the day of the **Equinox**, the **Sun** traversing the semi-circumference of the **Equator**—which is a great circle—travels one hundred and eighty degrees, or three hundred and sixty apparent feet. The diameter of a circle being approximately one-third of its circumference, or two-thirds of its semi-circumference, I shall have two hundred and forty feet for the diameter of a circle for which I have found a semi-circumference of three hundred and sixty feet. This exploit had a success much greater than **Sethos** himself had imagined. The first **Soldiers** who escaped alive from the two towers through the bottom gate cried out in a terrified tone that genies <note>original: "génies"; supernatural spirits or guardian deities, often thought to intervene in human affairs.</note> hostile to the **Thebans** had just descended from **Heaven** into the top of the towers, were slaughtering their comrades there, and were causing a dreadful havoc. This idea, supported by the cries of the men or by the noise of the falling planks, caused all those who had been stationed nearby to flee far from these buildings; and they did not fear to say that signs from **Heaven** were superior even to the orders of their **King**. **Mephrès**, who had seen the young men pass through the air, and who found it difficult to conceive of this unheard-of example of boldness—of which he well suspected that **Sethos** was the author—sensed clearly that he would not be believed if he alleged it. Thus, so as not to compromise his authority, he preferred to yield to the superstition of his **Army**. He ordered that very day that fire be set from a distance to the two towers, since they were displeasing to the **Gods**. He even added that since the great engines <note>original: "machines"; in this context, the heavy wooden siege towers used to scale city walls.</note> had not succeeded, they would no longer employ...

The King, however, formed that very day a Council composed of men who were reasonably well-intentioned. This Council would maintain the Kingdom, during the first years that followed, in a middle state between prosperity and weakness; but because this state leaned a bit more toward the latter than the former, it would allow the kingdom to reach the very brink of ruin during a foreign war, which will be the principal subject of the final book of this History.

## *BOOK SIX.*

Sethos, whom we shall call **CHERES** throughout the course of his Travels, in accordance with the name he had given himself, found upon arriving at the White Port <note>Known in antiquity as Leucos Limen, a major trading port on the Red Sea.</note> a fleet of fifteen ships, manned by ten thousand Phoenicians <note>The Phoenicians were the preeminent mariners of the ancient world, often employed by the Egyptian Pharaohs for their naval expertise.</note>. The Kings of Egypt, according to several testimonies of antiquity, made use of them to trade with foreign peoples, and to pilot their own vessels in distant seas. After having fruitlessly attempted to cut through the Isthmus that separates the Mediterranean from the Red Sea <note>The precursor to the modern Suez Canal.</note>; they had limited themselves to canals that could only accommodate vessels of mediocre size. Thus it had been necessary to lend the Phoenicians some ports on the Red Sea; and it was through these that the latter maintained communication with the Indies. One is alerted to the proximity of this admirable country long before discovering the land; and <term>Diodorus<gloss>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE known for his monumental universal history.</gloss></term> expresses himself on this subject in a very eloquent manner. Nothing, he says, equals the pleasure that this composite scent gives even to those who sail along this shore, and who only receive it from afar. The offshore winds carry these precious exhalations from the heart of the country out onto the Sea. They seep, so to speak, into the very depths of the soul; and emerging as they do from the very bosom of nature, they give travelers an idea of the <term>Ambrosia<gloss>In Greek mythology, the fragrant food or drink of the gods that granted immortality.</gloss></term> that Fable says serves the Gods.

They finally found themselves in the Strait where Cherès heard some members of the Crew say that until recently, it was believed to be closed. In fact, a certain <term>Damastes<gloss>Damastes of Sigeum, a 5th-century BCE Greek geographer and historian.</gloss></term> cited in <term>Strabo<gloss>An ancient Greek geographer whose work "Geographica" is a vital source for ancient world knowledge.</gloss></term> had held this opinion. This newly discovered passage was given an ill-omened name, being called *Sthenæ Deiræ* <note>original: "Sthenæ Deiræ", meaning the "Narrows of Dire."</note>, the "fatal strait," whether for the promontory of Ethiopia that overlooks it, or the Islands found there. Some Authors have even named it *Ostium luctus* <note>original: "Ostium luctus"</note>, the **Gate of Mourning**. It is not that it is extremely difficult or dangerous to cross; but in those early times when long voyages were very hazardous, it was indicated by this name that those who had the boldness to pass this strait to go further ran the risk of never returning.

The Peoples of **Taprobane** <note>The ancient Greek and Roman name for the island of Sri Lanka.</note> had a custom in naval combat that gave their courage an air of ferocity and despair, and which was sometimes fatal to them. They never boarded an enemy **Vessel** without attempting to hook it to their own with <term>iron grappling hooks</term> <note>original: "crampons de fer"</note> made specifically for this purpose; so that even had they wished to do so afterward, they would have had great difficulty detaching themselves. Thus, the defeated **Vessel** was necessarily captured by the other. **Cherès**, informed of this custom, resolved to take advantage of it. The Commander, after having settled the general arrangements for the battle in his presence, declared that he was sending him wherever he wished to go, to command on his behalf whatever he himself judged appropriate, until a signal to the contrary was given. But even if he had not granted him this authority, it would have come to him naturally more than once on every **Vessel** where he found himself. For in intense and perilous moments, the most confident and skilled man is always the one whom others follow. **Cherès**, nevertheless leaving to the Officers everywhere all the honor and the full scope of their duties, merely indicated to them what was necessary to assist him in the ventures he would undertake alone, as a simple soldier.

He had them brought to him, and despite their gaunt and pale faces, he recognized them as two officers who had formerly served under him; he then locked himself alone with them in the <term>council chamber</term>. The eldest said to him: "My Lord, we come here as deputies from **Pheletès**, the Chief of our **Colony**, who six months ago undertook an enterprise that seemed advantageous to our nation."

He judged it appropriate, before going to clear these shores of so many assassins, to form at the promontory a trade depot <note>The original term "entrepôt" refers to a commercial center or warehouse used for the storage and distribution of goods, essential for the expansion of Phoenician trade.</note> for his fleet, which would remain for the use of the Phoenicians. ->S E T H O S,<-

an example of their recent ferocity. Cherès <note>The pseudonym used by the Egyptian Prince Sethos.</note> told them that a great distinction had to be made between crimes committed by individuals against established laws in a civilized Nation, and practices born of the ignorance and coarseness of an entire People. He argued that the penalties they would be made to suffer before receiving instruction would be a forbidden vengeance and not a legitimate punishment. He did not feel any scruple about exterminating men who were harmful to the human race; and on this principle, he felt no regret for the slaughter they had made of the thirty Savages <note>This term reflects the 18th-century Eurocentric perspective of the author, Jean Terrasson, toward indigenous populations.</note> who guarded the stable, because he believed it then to be necessary. But now that he better understood the character of these Barbarians, he would consider himself very guilty to destroy a Nation that he was going to make useful through its labors to the <term>Phoenicians</term> <note>Ancient seafaring people from the Levant, depicted here as Sethos’s allies in establishing trade outposts.</note> themselves, and by extension of their commerce, to all the Peoples of the earth.

They dodged one sword only to meet another. They felt defeated at the first onset, and their resistance lasted hardly as long as my description of it. They stretched out their arms to beg for mercy; and the combat ceasing immediately, they were led by the thousands to the Ships, where they were put in irons. He granted to the Ethiopians <note>original: "Ethiopiens," a term used broadly in this period for the peoples of sub-Saharan Africa.</note> an amnesty by which he guaranteed not only their lives, but favorable treatment to all the Savages of the country, provided they renounced their former barbarity and acknowledged themselves as slaves of the Phoenicians. He had them placed together by families, promising them, in his name and in that of the Phoenicians their masters, that he would always keep them joined together in this way in the labors that would be imposed upon them. He excepted from this rule only the young men who were not yet married, whom he turned into Rowers in place of those he had brought from Taprobane <note>The ancient name for the island of Sri Lanka.</note>, converting the latter into Soldiers to swell the ranks of his troops. But he promised both groups of these new Captives to release them all once there were sufficient proofs of their fidelity. These acts of kindness on the part of a victor who had appeared so terrible to them, consoled them somewhat for their defeat and their enslavement. Those whom he left in their own country resigned themselves with less regret to these labors, which were ranked among the punishments of criminals, but to which many other men submit voluntarily for the sole purpose of earning a living. I am speaking of the mines that he had them open in the territory of Sophir <note>A region often identified with the biblical Ophir, famous for its gold.</note>, where Cherès arrived without any opposition, while freeing along the way all the Captives of the Anthropophagites <note><term>Anthropophagites</term>: a term derived from Greek meaning "eaters of humans," used historically to describe tribes believed to practice cannibalism.</note>.

The Egyptian Priests <margin>{</margin> taught them that mercury <note>mercury: historically called quicksilver, used here in the process of "amalgamation" to bind with precious metals.</note> poured over stone that had been simply crushed would bind itself to the precious metal. They showed how easy it was to then separate this amalgam—or mixture—from the sand or gravel that still clogged it; and finally, that it was simply a matter of evaporating the mercury over a fire, leaving the pure gold at the bottom of the vessel *. They added that this property of mercury also applied to silver, but had no effect on base metals <note>original: "metaux inferieurs," or non-precious metals like iron or lead.</note>, with which it would not bond. At the mines of Sophir <note>Sophir: a variation of Ophir, a legendary biblical land famed for its gold and riches.</note>, they were concerned only with the former. It is well known that in the following centuries, these mines provided the most celebrated nations not only with the gold used to gild the temples of their Gods and the palaces of their Kings, but also with the countless precious stones with which their women adorned themselves. Aside from those stones whose names are common, it was from there that they obtained the **pantarbe** <note>A legendary gemstone mentioned in ancient Greek literature, said to have magnetic properties or the ability to resist fire.</note>, which was said to have the power to repel the heat of fire, and the **sideropoecile** of the **Siderite** <note>Siderite: from the Greek for "iron-like." But as soon as navigation was first attempted, the great men of Egypt—such as Cecrops, Cadmus, and Danaus <note>Legendary figures in Greek mythology believed to have brought Egyptian or Phoenician culture, writing, and laws to Greece.</note>—exposed themselves to the fortunes of the sea, established colonies upon its shores, and were thereby the fathers of commerce, that amiable bond of society between distant nations. The heroes of Greece—Hercules, Theseus, and Pirithous—who lived shortly before Sethos, succeeded in this rivalry; and not content with making the seas known, they invited their contemporaries to frequent them by exterminating the pirates who crossed them and the tyrants who rendered the shores inaccessible. As each century has its dominant spirit, the only concern then among men who sought a high reputation was to find new countries, to build cities there, and to give laws to their inhabitants. But this practice having since been suspended, or at least greatly weakened, and these heroes having had, moreover, no historians but poets, it is not surprising that only faint traces of their routes remain to us. The anecdotes I employ propose nothing that is not plausible, by attributing specifically to Sethos what known authors indicate in general terms; that is, when they say that the Phoenicians, taught the art of navigation by the Egyptians, rounded the tip of Africa before all other peoples and as early as the Heroic Ages <note>The "Heroic Age" refers to the semi-mythological period of Greek and Egyptian history, typically associated with figures like Hercules or the Trojan War.</note>.

Our historians—the oldest of whom, according to Herodotus, only began to appear around the time of Xerxes's <note>King of Persia who invaded Greece in 480 BCE.</note> descent into Greece—our geographers, and our travel writers, who are even more recent than our historians, report or establish authorities themselves which all tend to prove that the circumnavigation of Africa was achieved more than once in the following centuries. It is true that some of them refute these authorities even while citing them. However, these refutations, repeated in several places in their works, prove at the very least that a continuous and sometimes renewed tradition always presents this fact as reality. Herodotus <margin>Book 4.</margin>, for example, recounts that Necho <note>Necho II, a Pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty (r. 610–595 BCE).</note>, that King of Egypt who was dethroned and killed by the Ethiopian Sabacon <note>Historically, Shabaka (Sabacon) lived earlier than Necho II; the author likely refers to the conflict between the 25th (Nubian/Ethiopian) and 26th (Sais) Dynasties.</note> four or five hundred years after Sethos, being curious to know the general layout of the seas and lands, sent Phoenicians on this voyage of discovery. As soon as the workers arrived, Cherès had work begin on the fortress; and as he wished to see it completed, he had the time to receive the response and the thanks of Astarte <note>The Queen of Egypt.</note>; after which he set back to sea and began to follow the coastline, sailing North. Following the method they had observed on the other side <note>The eastern coast of Africa.</note>, they stopped first at the river *of the Mountains*, and then at that *of the Elephants*, names derived from the local geography. The inhabitants up to the Tropic were found to be much like those of the corresponding Eastern coast. He named those closest to the Cape the *Grigriquas* and those closest to the Tropic the *Namaquas*. And throughout this entire expanse, the Phoenicians did not deign to establish any settlement or trade.

In continuing their route, they saw a little above the Southern Tropic a very large river (*the Bravaghul*.) Cherès did not require them to make a landing there, because this river was surrounded by terrifying deserts to the right and left, as far as the eye could see. ...to navigate; Cherès had trumpeters and kettledrums climb onto the two prows, playing for an hour the liveliest and most cheerful tunes ever composed in Phoenicia <note>Phoenicia was an ancient civilization located along the coast of the Levant, renowned in antiquity for its maritime skill and music.</note>. It is poor policy for great merchants to seek to impoverish their neighbors; all the more so because they thereby lose the market for their own goods, which their neighbors are no longer in a position to buy. In the context of this 18th-century novel, this refers to the indigenous African population Sethos is organizing into a new society.</note> were permitted to settle in the countryside however they saw fit; while striving, nonetheless, to gather at the center of several estates to form villages—something that inhabitants of any country do naturally, drawn also by the convenience of rivers and main roads. However, they were forbidden from ever settling in the City by purchasing houses, the elegance of which did not suit the initial education they had received; or by establishing themselves there as workers or craftsmen, as the Phoenician Colony <note>The "Phoenician Colony" refers to the group of Mediterranean settlers Sethos led to Africa, who possessed advanced technical and architectural skills.</note> already had enough of its own nation; or finally, by offering themselves to the White inhabitants <note>original: "Blancs." Referring here to the Phoenician settlers.</note> as voluntary servants, which would place them in a state of degradation from which they ought to keep themselves. The White inhabitants could purchase slaves for their own use from the Colony of Sophir <note>Sophir is a variant of "Ophir," the legendary biblical land famous for its gold and riches, often associated with East Africa or the Indian Ocean.</note>, or even from the inhabitants of the Congo who also engaged in this trade. But the Black inhabitants were forbidden from owning slaves. By this, he wished to encourage them to always work with their own hands, or to secure help by producing children and grandchildren through early marriages. But regardless of this assistance, he did not forbid them from having voluntary servants from among their own nation.

Not content with this initial fund for the King, he established a tenth <note>A tithe or 10% tax on production.</note> on all the revenues of the countryside. This is a type of tax which, being levied equitably and taking the place of all others, never increases except to the satisfaction of the taxpayer, following the reflection of the Advocate of the Sicilians against Verres <note>original: "l'Avocat des Siciliens contre Verres." A reference to the Roman orator Cicero and his famous legal pursuit of Gaius Verres, a corrupt governor of Sicily. Cicero suggested that a higher tax yield from a fair percentage is a sign of a farmer's success, not his oppression.</note>; because it is a sign that he has become wealthier. But furthermore, it reveals to a wise Prince the true strength of his State. Moreover, he judged that moderate impositions stimulate the work of the husbandman <note>original: "Laboureur," referring to the agricultural worker.</note>, who without this goad would soon fall into idleness, and consequently into poverty. He did not wish to prescribe anything regarding duties on merchandise. This was a point on which the Phoenician Colonies already had their own customs. He only specifically warned the Viceroy not to hinder a trade that was just beginning to be born, and not to place an obstacle in the way of a future and imminent abundance for the sake of a present gain of little consequence.

Finally, Cherès believed he should also consider the interests of the Egyptian Priests. He emphasized the modesty of this portion, which amounted to only nine-hundredths of the revenue of the countryside, in comparison to the third of all assets they possessed in Egypt; and he announced the use that their customary magnificence would lead them to make of the little attributed to them, through temples and other buildings that would beautify the new Phoenicia.

He established schools in the City where the sciences were not to be carried as far as in Egypt; and only those sciences that might suit merchant navigators were to be taught there. He entrusted their care to the Phoenician priests. However, he did not wish to establish any schools in the countryside. Following the constant maxim of the Egyptians, who remained from father to son in the same profession, he believed that the same mental occupations that keep the children of noble families from idleness instead throw the children of husbandmen <note>Agricultural workers.</note>, and even of laborers, into it. In his view, all study was an enemy of manual labor and corrupted the spirit of those whom birth had destined for the <term>mechanical arts</term> <note>Manual trades and crafts, which were historically distinguished from the "liberal arts."</note>.

Rectifying, nonetheless, what was too general in that exclusion <note>Referring to the exclusion of schools from the countryside mentioned on the previous page, intended to keep the peasantry focused on agriculture.</note>, he allowed the Priests to instruct in their own homes those in whom they perceived a marked talent for something superior to the cultivation of the land.

It was in this way that Cherès, after having been the victor and benefactor of the savages of the Congo, became further their Legislator. When he was on the point of departure, he made the Viceroy solemnly swear that these laws—written out at length along with their underlying motives and published throughout the entire extent of the Viceroyalty—would be observed; and that they would not be changed according to needs or the passage of time, except in the very spirit of their original institution. He particularly recommended to him, in the tables <note>Referring to the physical tablets or formal legal documents where the laws were inscribed.</note> he had made, those inhabitants coming from the Congo; and he required that favor should always be shown to them in all doubtful or ambiguous matters they might have with the Phoenicians or their other associates, for the very reason of the inferiority of their enlightenment and knowledge. There is every appearance that the Viceroys who succeeded Aferyme, taking advantage—as usually happens—of the great distance they felt from the King their master, soon violated the oath of their predecessor; and that, having used their authority tyrannically, they were driven out a few years later by the savages. This is evidenced by the fact that the memory of such a fine establishment has been preserved only in my anecdotal authors <note>The narrator refers to "private" or "unpublished" historical sources, a common literary device in 18th-century novels to explain why certain "events" aren't in standard history books.</note>, and that one finds everywhere else only confused traces of the great number of colonies that the Phoenicians held upon the coasts of every sea.

### BOOK VII.

Cherès was ready to set sail to continue his journey when he received a packet from Astarte. The latter sent him the original of a letter from the King, in which the King expressed his admiration and gratitude toward this extraordinary man, who had already brought the fruits of his establishments as far as Phoenicia, and whose benefactions had spread his reputation. The King added that he did not address his thanks directly to Cherès, in order to follow the channel that this illustrious stranger had chosen by addressing himself only to Astarte, and so as not to pull aside the veil under which he seemed to wish to hide <note>Cherès, who is actually the Egyptian prince Sethos, travels incognito to perform his deeds without the burden of his royal identity.</note>. But he joyfully ratified all the arrangements, all the institutions, and all the appointments that he had made, and that he might make in the course of his discoveries. He specifically confirmed Aseryme <note>In the previous section, this name was spelled Aferyme; such variations in spelling are common in 18th-century texts.</note> in the Vice-royalty of New Phoenicia, and, on the advice and at the urging of Astarte, gave him the Stewardship of Western trade <term>Intendance du commerce: The administrative oversight and management of all merchant activities and maritime exchange in the region.</term>.

Cherès replied to Astarte that, not having the honor of being personally known to the King, he had not believed it appropriate to trouble him with a letter signed with a name as insignificant as his own. He added that there was no enterprise that would not be easy with Officers and soldiers as wise, as courageous, and as skilled as those who composed the Phoenician Fleet. He concluded by saying that he regarded this letter as the last he would write to Astarte before returning to Egypt; and thus, the King of Phoenicia would necessarily know the conclusion of their voyage before he did.

But his true intention in this delay was to allow his face to change, which, necessarily losing the bloom of youth over a few years since the age of sixteen, would become unrecognizable to all those who had not seen him during that interval. This was also *Cherès’s* thought in prolonging his absence, and they both intended to surprise the Court of *Memphis*—the former through imposture, and the latter through truth. But *Cherès* will only receive the first news of this competitor on the coasts of the *Mediterranean*.

# BOOK VII.

...of Three Points, which both sides had chosen as a neutral location where they came twice a year to conduct their exchanges. The Phoenicians were particularly interested in the gold that the Black Africans <note>original: "Negres"</note> drew in abundance from the Gold Coast and the shores of Elmina <note>original: "la Mine"; referring to the region of São Jorge da Mina in modern-day Ghana, famous for its gold trade.</note>. Cherès’s intention was to inspire the inhabitants of Guinea with a little more openness and confidence in trade, and to encourage them to welcome other nations more freely into their territory. 

As they already knew how to trade, they had only this one step remaining to cease being savages. For this status <note>original: "défaut" (defect/lack)</note> consists in ignoring the existence of other peoples or in avoiding their company; just as simple barbarism consists in having no knowledge of letters. Savages have no connection in the present world; and barbarians, though otherwise capable of treaties and even social interaction with foreigners, remain deprived of the communication that reading provides to refined nations with people of all eras. 

But Cherès did not want to begin anything on this subject except in the capital, which always dictates the law or serves as a model for the rest of a state. He postponed his undertaking there all the more readily because he heard it said that the King of Guinea, though still young, was working to shape the character and customs of his subjects. He finally arrived at Accra <note>original: "Acara"</note> with his entire fleet, guided in some way by the leaders of the Black Africans <note>original: "Negres"</note> whom he had brought on board with him.

The King having proposed this difficulty to Cherès, Cherès first replied that he admired the insight with which the King had realized that Kings are hardly masters of a false sense of honor <note>original: "point d'honneur"</note> that has unfortunately taken hold of their subjects' minds. This Egyptian style of ritual was not entirely unknown in Guinea. Not only had Phoenician commerce brought its reputation to them, but they also knew through the traditions of their neighbors that the Egyptian Hercules <note>Egyptian Hercules: Likely a reference to the god Shu or Herishef, whom the Greeks and later writers identified with Hercules; he was often credited in legends with traveling to the edges of the known world.</note>, one of the first initiates, had traveled as far as the strait of the two seas <note>The "strait of the two seas" likely refers to the Strait of Gibraltar, often cited in antiquity as the "Pillars of Hercules."</note>. 

The King was very pleased with this proposal. Having shared it with some of his most faithful and intelligent servants, they all gave him hope that his people would joyfully receive an institution borrowed from the most famous nation on earth, brought to their country by Egyptians themselves. Furthermore, it would deliver them from the long durations, the sufferings, and above all, the fatal consequences of the Initiation of the Jannanes.

The Fetiferos, having recognized from the King’s tone and gaze that he intended to be obeyed, kept to a course of silence for a long time, which was the safest path for them. They even suspended all public exercise of their religion and left the King, Cherès, and the Egyptians in peace for about six months, which the latter employed in the manner we shall briefly relate.

These Priests <note>The group of Egyptian priests who accompanied the protagonist.</note> had entered Acara <note>A kingdom or region in Guinea described in the narrative.</note> only six in number. But having already had time to foresee that they would need assistance in the execution of their enterprise, they had easily obtained from the King the freedom to send for fifteen or sixteen of their colleagues, who were settled, according to their custom, within the Phoenician Colony established at Cape Palmas, which belongs to Guinea. Thus, they numbered more than twenty at the start of their labors. They had all agreed with Cherès—who was Sethos <note>Sethos is the hero’s true name; he travels under the alias Cherès to maintain his anonymity during his travels.</note> to them—that it was necessary to present the inhabitants of Guinea with an Initiation less mysterious, less heroic even, and more general than that of Egypt. This was because the Egyptian Initiation, being established in a nation that otherwise possessed all the necessary aids for common virtue, derived its value from being accessible only to extraordinary men; whereas an Initiation presented to a people still in a savage state <note>original: "Sauvage" — In this 18th-century context, the author uses this term to describe a society that has not yet adopted the laws, sciences, or "refined" religious structures of civilizations like Egypt.</note>, and who required every kind of instruction, would only be useful if it admitted at least all the youth who were not yet sworn to evil spirits,

The Egyptian priests would consecrate this Temple to the Goddess of Virtues, to which all young people of both sexes who had reached the age of fifteen were invited to come in advance to be initiated.

This plan was faithfully executed; and although it contained nothing but what was very simple, the instructions alone produced a marvelous effect on the minds of all these people. As the day’s sixteen discourses were given in the two Chapelles on the same subjects by sixteen different Priests, and since each of the listeners had only heard two of them; they were seen gathering in small groups in the streets themselves, to ask one another what they had heard, and to make comparisons.

Regarding every eighth day, on which entry to the chapels was forbidden to the <term>profane: The uninitiated public</term>; the primary motive for this exception was to preserve some appearance of the secrecy of the Egyptian Initiation, and to provide some encouragement to the initiates. For otherwise, the secret here did not concern any outward curiosity, and it was directed solely toward the moral benefit of the aspirants. They were taught that animal sacrifices did not please the Divinity in and of themselves. That the Divinity particularly hated incisions made upon one's own body—which were believed to be so pleasing to evil spirits <note>original: "mauvais esprits"</note>. That it was the vices whose roots had to be cut, and the passions of the heart that had to be quelled within oneself. That the moderate fasting prescribed for everyone during the time of preparation was a sign of this detachment, a means of achieving it, and a restitution <note>original: "satisfaction"</note> owed for the disorders into which one had fallen before undertaking it.

This language, of which Phoenician trade had already given them some notion, but which was not common <note>original: "vulgaire," meaning the everyday vernacular of the local people</note> to them, was to be the language of the books made to instruct the Priests, and even that of the Rites of the future Temple, in order to preserve more dignity for them. But the explanations of these Rites, as well as instructions of every kind, were always to be given to the People in the common tongue. To further encourage these new disciples in the work that lay before them, their teachers declared that they only wished to exercise the functions of both Priests and Masters in Guinea for five years, and until the upcoming Initiation which would be scheduled at that interval by a rule that would remain in place forever. It would then be up to them to preside over this Initiation, to bear its fruits over time throughout the Kingdom, and finally to train their own successors themselves.

# BOOK VII

...of their punishment. This was not Cherès’s intention, and he fully intended to have the sentence softened. But he wanted to let them endure all the terror they only too well deserved. Meanwhile, they were led to the royal prisons to the satisfaction of all the people.

The children of the Fetiseros <term>Fetiseros: A term used in this narrative for the deceptive priests or sorcerers, likely derived from the Portuguese "feiticeiro"</term>, learning this news in the palace, fell into a consternation all the greater because, before their initiation into the Jannanes <note>The Jannanes were the secret order of "spirits" the Fetiseros pretended to be</note>, their fathers never made them participants in the secret of their impostures. Cherès, who wished to accompany the King as far as his palace, took advantage of the touching sight of these weeping youths to move him to compassion. He represented to him that young men destined for the priesthood of the Goddess of Virtues needed a reputation beyond reproach. He argued that there was reason to hope, from their zeal for public service and the purity of their religion, that they would repair the crimes and superstitions of the Fetiseros; but that nothing would erase, in the eyes of a coarse populace, the stain of their fathers' execution. "The punishment of parents," he added, "dishonors even the most innocent families in the eyes of common men more than the gravest faults dishonor the guilty themselves when they go unpunished." 

The King replied immediately that since he had only wanted to sacrifice the Fetiseros to the vengeance of the Goddess of Virtues, he would desist from this sacrifice as soon as it was no longer pleasing to her. Thus, he left it to Cherès to find the most appropriate means to ensure, at the very least, that these wretches could never again disturb either the worship of the Goddess or the peace of his subjects.

### BOOK VII.

E

<meta>Volume II; catchword: One</meta>

The interactions the inhabitants of this city had with the Phoenicians of the fleet had taught them that this nation, far from harming their trade, was very capable of enhancing it—not only through its extensive connections but also through its intelligence and advice. Thus, before the end of the second year, all the ports of **Acara** <note>Modern-day Accra, in Ghana.</note> were open to the Phoenicians of **Cape Palmas** <note>Located in modern Liberia.</note>; and the **Cape of Three Points** was no longer a barrier between the two peoples. Egyptian priests also multiplied on this occasion throughout **Guinea**. And **Cherès** <note>The name Sethos uses while in disguise.</note>, not forgetting the assistance needed by those he had left in the **Congo** and in **New Phoenicia**, sent some of these priests to them, without anyone having the trouble of going to fetch more from **Memphis**. This is also what provided him the means, when the day of his departure arrived, to take with him—without hindering the service in Guinea—the six priests remaining of the ten he had embarked on his fleet when leaving **Taprobane** <note>The ancient Greek name for the island of Sri Lanka.</note>. As they had never lost sight of him since the day they recognized him at **Galiba**, and as his face had only changed imperceptibly to them, they were precious witnesses for him for the time when he might judge it appropriate to reveal his true identity.

I shall not recount here the regrets he left behind in **Acara** on the day he set sail to continue his route. He would have been moved by them himself, had he not armed himself early on with the thought that he was but a traveler who must not attach himself to anything on his path, and who was not permitted to taste the sweetness of his own good deeds in foreign lands.

# S E T H O S,

He was warned at the **Cape of Three Points** <note>A peninsula in modern-day Ghana.</note> that to travel to **Cape Palmas** <note>Located on the coast of modern Liberia.</note>, and even to visit the coast as far as the **Strait of Hercules** <note>The Strait of Gibraltar, which connects the Atlantic Ocean to the Mediterranean Sea.</note>, it was necessary to take on, from place to place, **pilots** <term>local navigators</term> who knew the depths, the reefs, and above all the entrances to the ports, almost all of which had their own particular difficulties. Indeed, they had him keep to the high seas until the western point of **Cape Palmas**, where he saw on an elevation a small grove of palm trees *, which had caused the **Black inhabitants** <note>original: "Negres"</note> to give this name to the Cape. I find however in another of my authors that this name also came from the huts suspended from palm trees twenty and thirty feet above the ground, where the local people sought shelter from the humidity of the land, the persecution of insects, and the attacks of **raiders** † <note>original: "coureurs"; refers to local marauders or rival tribes.</note>. The **Phoenicians** and later the **Greeks**, as we have said beforehand, named this Cape the **Hesperian Horn** or point, the **Hesperian Horn** <note>original: *Hesperum cornu*</note>.

He then made himself master of all the land up to the **Zilis** river; and further seizing the Kingdom of **Atlas** from the interior of the lands, he left him little but the shores of the ocean from this river to the **Lesser Atlas**, upon which this King went sometimes to contemplate the stars. **Antaeus**, wanting to carry his invasion further, undertook to cross the **Zilis**. **Hercules**, at the head of a few boats laden with soldiers, easily repulsed him †. But having wanted to pursue him onto his own lands, **Antaeus** found himself supported by ever-new battalions; so that **Hercules**, having defeated his troops three times, found himself no further advanced than at the beginning of the battle. Thereupon, he judged it appropriate to re-embark. But to lure **Antaeus** to follow him, he first sent the greater part of his boats to the other shore. He ordered the soldiers to hide there behind the small woods that lined it. Thus **Antaeus**, seeing that **Hercules** was stepping out of his boat almost alone, had the temerity to step out of his own after him, accompanied by a sort of fleet such as one can imagine on a river. WHEN Cherès was preparing to launch a skiff <note>A small, light boat used for transport between a ship and the shore.</note> to send and ask the Governor of the port for permission to enter, he was himself anticipated by a flat-bottomed boat that came out to meet him to learn his name, his country, and his intentions. This Hero satisfied all the questions put to him with great sincerity and modesty. The representative, seeing that Cherès already knew their nation, dared to promise him on behalf of his King—who was currently in the port—the kind of reception that a man of his merit and reputation could expect from a people who prided themselves on loving and valuing virtue. Immediately, he had Cherès’s vessel attached to his own and, by force of oars, towed it into the basin which held a large number of foreign ships that the storm of previous days had forced to seek shelter there.

### BOOK VIII.

The Empire [of Antaeus] being of a suitable extent, he had for a long time set his sights on Carthage; for he believed it was necessary to reach that far to achieve a conquest of great renown. Two or three years ago, with this design in mind, he formed a secret league against the Carthaginians with the Kings of the two other Mauretanias <note>Mauretania: In antiquity, this referred to the Berber kingdoms of North Africa, not the modern country of Mauritania.</note>, the Massæsylian (called *Caesariensis* <note>original: "Cæsariensis"; Mauretania Caesariensis was a Roman province located in what is now central and western Algeria.</note> by the Romans), and the Sitifensian <note>Refers to the region around Sétif in modern Algeria.</note>. The conditions of this league were that the two Kings—who had been defeated and made tributaries of the Carthaginians by Saphon, the eldest son of Zoros, the Founder and Prince of Carthage <note>In this novel, the author creates a fictionalized early history of Carthage, naming Zoros as the founder rather than the traditional Queen Dido.</note>—would make no movement on their part that could make them suspicious to the Carthaginians. However, they would supply him from then on, and at regular intervals thereafter, certain sums of money to raise troops. When the time was right, they would secretly grant passage to these troops through their States. Finally, he took it upon himself to surprise and reduce Carthage by this route, and thus to free them from the unjust domination of this new Republic.

The treaty of these Kings remained unknown; and the placement of the troops from Tingitana within the two other Mauretanias was already well advanced when Zoros and his Senate were informed of it. The Republic seemed to possess, in the two sons of Zoros, Saphon and Giscon, the two captains of the world most capable of defending it. They themselves anticipated the request that was to be made of their services. But the Senate, judging it appropriate to attack the enemy in two places, resolved to separate their commissions. It was important that one of them defend the frontiers of the Carthaginian Empire

He therefore alleged to the Senate that since his eldest son was an inexorable victor and possessed at least as much of a spirit of conquest as Antaeus, he would feel much more inclined to invade the states of this King—using a pretext as plausible as the one being offered—than to cede to him any provinces of the Carthaginian Empire, however uncultivated, remote, or useless they might be.

The second son, on the contrary, having never attacked these peoples, was in no way hated by them. Furthermore, as he did not favor the enlargement of an Empire that he already found only too extensive, he was thereby much more disposed to present peace proposals to the enemy when it was deemed appropriate to offer them.

Moreover, the Republic of the Capsenses <note>Capsenses: The people of Capsa, an ancient city in modern-day Tunisia (modern Gafsa). In this novel, the city is depicted as being founded on idealized, heroic principles.</note> which he had founded through heroic labors and without any shadow of personal interest, gave him a reputation—if not of greater brilliance, then at least of greater credit—than that of his elder brother.

Finally, the advantage he had of returning to his homeland invested with the Egyptian Initiation <note>Egyptian Initiation: A reference to the sacred and secretive religious mysteries of ancient Egypt. In the context of this 18th-century novel, having passed these trials signifies a man of supreme moral character and wisdom.</note> had earned him extraordinary respect among all the Kings of Africa.

The Senate, after some representations, yielded to the views of its Prince; and fundamentally regarding his two sons as two great captains, though of different characters, it distributed the two commissions according to the desires of Zoros. **Gisco** learned on that same day of his brother’s death, the rout of his army, and the siege of **Carthage**. It was then that the horrific consequences of his crime made him feel their full weight. He realized that the reckless and forbidden compliance he had shown toward the enemy was the primary cause of his country’s misfortunes and the loss of his own innocence. He conceived for **Saphon**—who had been killed with his weapons in hand and in the glorious exercise of his duty—a respect he had not felt so deeply during his life; and the death of a brother with whom he had not been extremely close left him with all the regrets of the most tender and vivid friendship. 

But above all else, he was overwhelmed by the image of his father. He imagined the anxieties, the terrors, and the mortal agonies that this venerable old man was perhaps currently experiencing, as the only reward for the many marks of affection and trust Gisco had always received from him; even while he was overturning his father's Empire through a willful and fatal imprudence, and violating paternal rights through a hidden love and a secret marriage. # BOOK VIII.

The result of this was that our Temples were deserted during voluntary solemnities, and pretexts for dispensation <note>Legal or religious excuses to be exempt from a duty.</note> multiplied in others. Our High Priests, who are in a sense entrusted with the body of this same Religion, have always opposed this kind of reform. As leaders of society in such a considerable part, they have paid extreme attention to the multitude. The perfection of a few individuals is a private matter, of which the Priests whom one consults in secret and separately must take very great care. But one cannot impose this as a Law upon an entire People, among whom it is nevertheless important to maintain the love and habit of Religion. In a word, the maxims of our High Priests, and the success of their conduct, have convinced us that while a narrow mind attempts in vain to reduce the commonality of men to its own tastes, the great man leads them where he wishes by following theirs.

### BOOK VIII.

<sig>G 5</sig>

<meta>catchword: and</meta>

...North, and by a mountain range to the East. We do not seek to expand it either. And to tell the truth, our Laws would be too restrictive for a large Kingdom, where we could never maintain the union and uniformity that is the soul of our customs and practices. It is enough then to tell you that our King is elective, since Atlas <note>In the context of this novel, Atlas is portrayed as the historical founder of the Atlantean civilization, rather than just the mythological Titan who carries the sky.</note> our Founder, dying without any successor of his blood, chose one himself from among our Fellow Citizens. We require, following the model of this first electee, that the King be between fifty and sixty years old at the time of his election. Every Citizen, as well as every inhabitant of the countryside who has proven a certain fixed income, may be nominated; provided, however, that he is not the son of the deceased, or his closest relative if he had no son; which in this case excludes all nephews or all cousins of the same degree. Political maneuvering <note>original: "brigues" — refers to the 18th-century concept of factions, secret canvassing, or corrupt lobbying for office.</note> is absolutely forbidden; and it would even be quite useless, given the freedom and the secrecy of the ballot <term>scrutin: the method of voting by secret ballot to ensure impartiality.</term> cast solely by those Citizens who have passed the age of eligibility, but who otherwise were of a standing to be eligible themselves. Once named, the King is absolute master of the Government. But he takes an oath not to touch the Laws of the State, and to receive the representations of the assembled Magistrates whom he does not appoint, but whom he approves. He is also entreated on the day of his installation to retain all the Ministers of his predecessor who are capable of fulfilling their duties. It is there that the exchange is made, without speaking and without seeing one another <note>This describes "silent trade" or "dumb barter," a practice famously attributed to the Carthaginians and West African tribes by Herodotus, where goods were exchanged without direct verbal communication to ensure peace and security.</note>, for the merchandise brought to us by the **Phoenicians**, in the manner they surely recounted to you themselves at Banausa. Thus our **Merchants**, receiving their goods only from these **Commissioners**, retail them only to our **Citizens** at a price that is never stated more than once. They are also permitted to deliver goods to foreigners like yourselves for your own use: but you will see their practices in this regard if you wish to provide yourselves with anything beneath the pillars of **Lixa** <note>Likely referring to Lixus, an ancient Phoenician and later Roman city in Morocco, legendary for its massive stone structures and connections to the Hesperides.</note>. This Temple, like all the buildings of Lixa <note>original: "Lixa"; an ancient city on the Atlantic coast of modern-day Morocco, traditionally associated with the Hesperides</note>, was orderly, well-designed, and well-constructed, but without any architectural ornament. Upon leaving there, it was the foreigners themselves who asked permission to go and greet the King, which was granted to them. 

They were then led to all the places in this first part of the city that their guides judged would give them the most pleasure. They did not forget to have them rest from time to time under porticoes that were more comfortable than grand, where other Atlantes gathered to converse on all sorts of honorable and useful subjects. As one was never alone there, the Citizens were permitted to engage in conversation even with the foreigners; and the latter noted the discretion of the Atlantes in not wearying them with questions, being content with whatever they chose to say of their own accord. 

Having returned to the guest house to spend the great heat of the day there, they set out three hours later to go to the other part of the city. They crossed the river on a bridge of boats that opened to allow passage for the Atlantes' vessels; for no other people used this river within the extent of their territory. Our foreigners...

# SETHOS,

They noticed that as the evening began, there were many women with the men under the porticoes. Their guides told them that the only women present were those capable of engaging in conversation with the men. This advice inspired their curiosity to draw closer to them. They observed that the women listened with an attention that encouraged those who reasoned soundly; they understood subtle points well, and they spoke less than the men, but with greater ease.

Such an entertaining sight led Cherès to say that knowing a city did not consist of knowing the extent of its plan, nor the number and form of its buildings, but that one must study its inhabitants and be able to describe the inner life of its society <note>original: "l’interieur de la société"; referring to the private social dynamics and domestic manners that define a culture</note>. He added that this inner life depended greatly in every country upon the spirit of the women and the manner in which they were treated.

"However," he said to his guides, "we would very much like not to end the day without learning how strangers who come to buy something are received here. The practices of your Subur market <note>Subur: likely a reference to a specific commercial district within Lixa, or perhaps a literary allusion to the Subura in Rome, known for its bustling trade</note> and some general conversations we have heard make us suspect something singular in your customs regarding this matter." 

Their guides replied that it was up to them to learn this for themselves. They pointed out the largest market hall in Lixa, which, due to its construction, was called the Hall of the Great Pillars; and to allow them the pleasure of a surprise, the guides would let them go there alone, while they waited under the same portico where they currently stood.

We act differently toward passengers whom storms or shipwrecks have cast into our port or upon our coasts: For on the eve of their departure, the King, assisted by the first of his Ministers and the Overseer of their guest house, settles accounts with them—not for the expenses we may have incurred for the treatment of their men, healthy or sick, or for the refitting of their ships; but for the damages they have suffered, and the money they need to reach the place where they are headed. They are given money quite often; and if anything is received from them, it is in proportion to what remains to them, and not to what they have spent. 

This selflessness <note>original: "désintéressement"; a lack of self-interest or a spirit of altruism</note> only served to inflame the liberality of Cherès and his two companions: For having returned to their guest house, all three agreed together that the two officers, upon leaving the port, would throw into the box ten times <note>original: "le décuple"</note> their expenses, which they calculated among themselves; saying that it was the least share they could give to the Atlanteans <note>original: "Atlantes"; the inhabitants of the legendary land described in the narrative</note> from the treasures they brought from Sophir <note>likely a reference to Ophir, the fabled biblical port famous for its gold and wealth</note>. ### BOOK VIII.

...try to pull him <note>Giscon is referring here to his father, Hamilcar, or perhaps the personification of his Country/the Senate.</note> from the abyss where I have plunged him; and your wisdom will soon make you understand that it would be impossible for me to present him with a wife whom he would regard as the source of all his misfortunes. I only dare to beg you not to detain me here for your vengeance; entrust it to the justice of the Senate of Carthage; and do not take away the means for me to return to my duty before my approaching death.

Giscon was indeed leaving, when the Princess ran to him, and stopping him, said: "Unfortunate Giscon, I clearly recognize your fall by the blindness that accompanies the very plan you have to raise yourself from it. You have betrayed your country and your father; and you believe you can appease the Gods by renouncing your wife. It is a consequence of crime that it is not always easy to escape it, or that one cannot abandon its object <note>original: "l'objet." In 18th-century French literature, the "object" of one's affection or crime refers to the person involved.</note> as soon as one wishes. # SETHOS.

## BOOK NINE.

CHERÈS <note>The pseudonym used by the Egyptian prince Sethos throughout much of his travels.</note>, while visiting all his vessels one after another, found them replenished with men, supplies, and everything they might have lacked upon arriving at Banasa <note>A historical city in Mauretania Tingitana, located in modern-day Morocco. It was a vital trade hub for the Phoenicians and later the Romans.</note>. They had, above all, replaced the horses, of which a greater proportion had been lost than men throughout the entire course of the voyage. And it is noteworthy that of all working animals, man is the one who resists the longest against fatigue, the deprivation of ordinary food, and changes in climate. The two officers had performed their commission with great zeal; and without being accused of having revealed their commander’s secret, the Phoenicians <note>The famous maritime traders of the ancient world who established colonies along the North African coast.</note> of the fleet, as well as those of Banasa, had strongly suspected that the love of justice alone would drive him against Antaeus <note>A legendary giant and king of Libya, often depicted in Greek mythology as the son of Poseidon and Gaia. In this narrative, he represents a tyrannical force.</note>. They had learned more specific news of this King from the ships of their compatriots who had arrived at the port of this colony in the interval of

It is true that the council of Banasa <note>The OCR text reads "Banafa," likely a misreading of the "long s" common in older typography for the city of Banasa.</note> did not permit any Phoenician residing there to enlist on this occasion. As the Kings of Tingitana <note>A reference to the region of Mauretania Tingitana in North Africa.</note> had granted the city and a large territory in sovereignty to the colony, in the hope they conceived of the advantages that Phoenician commerce would bring them, the council did not judge it prudent or equitable to allow its inhabitants to take up arms against them. But it permitted the passing Phoenicians to supply themselves there with everything they believed necessary for an expedition that had not even been declared. Cherès, having then assembled the Council of War, first proposed the general plan of bringing aid to the Carthaginians. All those present replied that the entire fleet had already predisposed itself to this proposal before it was even made; and that the crews would be very distressed if their expectations and courage were disappointed in this regard. "This being so," said Cherès, "I believe that our first exploit must be to go and help the Carthaginians press the siege of Siga <note>An important ancient maritime city located in modern-day Algeria, then part of the Numidian kingdom.</note>; for by leaving only a suitable garrison in that city after its capture, we will lead the remainder of the besieging troops toward Carthage: And with them, along with the thirty thousand soldiers that your care has gathered in this fleet, we shall form a sufficiently numerous army." This plan was approved by the Council and received with unanimous applause on every ship where the news was sent.

->S E T H O S,<-

"It is not," continued Cherès before the Council still assembled, "that there does not occur to my mind an expedition prior to that one, and much closer at hand. The wind, being favorable, can put us in two days at the entrance of the strait <note>Likely the Strait of Gibraltar, known in antiquity as the Pillars of Hercules.</note>, and in sight of Tingi <note>Ancient Tingis, modern-day Tangier.</note>, the capital of King Antaeus. It is not a matter of forming a siege. It is an undertaking for which we have neither the troops nor the necessary machines; and which, even with such aid, would be too long, and would leave this King time to take Carthage. The same difficulty does not apply to Siga <note>A major Numidian port city.</note>, where the siege is already advanced; and whose capture will, moreover, have the advantage of increasing our army, which we would, on the contrary, have to diminish to leave a sufficient garrison in Tingi.

I limit myself, therefore, regarding this latter place, to giving it a passing assault <note>original: "insulte"—in 18th-century military terms, an 'insult' refers to a sudden, unexpected attack on a fortified position without a formal siege.</note> during the space of a single night, which might vex Antaeus and diminish the confidence with which he besieges the capital of the Carthaginian Empire. But to attempt this expedition with prudence, it would be well if we had some idea of the interior of this city, and the outlets by which we might surprise it more easily. I have already heard it said that the Phoenicians recently arrived at Banasa, and whose ships have been willing to join our fleet, had spent several months at Tingi to distribute their merchandise. If their captains, present here, would share with us what they observed during the stay they made there, we could all judge together whether something of what I have just proposed can be executed."

### B O O K IX.

The first of these Captains spoke first: That having been at Tingi <note>Ancient Tingis, modern-day Tangier.</note> when the first news of the siege of Siga <note>An ancient Numidian port and capital city.</note> was received there, they saw that the Governor was putting everyone in order and under strict rule. That he even had their ships suddenly inspected; where, having found only their ordinary armament, they had been left in peace. But that everything had slackened as soon as it was known that the siege of Siga had been suspended; and that the ever-increasing progress of Antaeus had finally caused everything to pass from relaxation to total dissolution. 

He added that since it had been learned that the battle of Tubusupte <note>An ancient city in North Africa, also known as Tubusuptu or Tiklat.</note> was won, and especially that the siege of Carthage had been formed by the King in person; nocturnal festivals had been established, during which the entire great square before the Palace of Antaeus was illuminated, and that one saw nothing on all sides but dancing and feasting. That every evening, the young Prince named Tygée, aged about twelve years, was brought there. We are not even certain that the forces of Tingitana <note>The Roman province of Mauretania Tingitana, roughly modern-day northern Morocco, where the city of Tingi (Tangier) was located.</note>, which we do not know, might not arrive soon and drive out our Garrison. In the context of this novel, he is depicted as the King of Libya and the primary antagonist threatening Carthage.</note> in particular would console himself for the loss of Tingi by the conquest of Carthage. After some consultation among the officers regarding all that had just been proposed, the most senior among them replied to Cherès: That under any commander other than him, the council would have difficulty consenting to an exploit as perilous for the leader himself as the one in question. But having witnessed the successful execution of all his projects, they could do no better than to trust in his leadership, and above all, in the favor with which the Gods had so far rewarded the uprightness and generosity of his intentions.

They therefore spent all the remaining time until the following evening preparing and coordinating an operation that could only succeed through very careful communication with one another. Cherès, speaking first in private to the two captains he had chosen as his guides, shared with them his desire to also bring along the two governors <note>The "Governors" here refers to the royal tutors or guardians responsible for the young Prince Tygée.</note>. Let us try to avoid the same misfortune regarding the two governors, which will be easy if they are unarmed. He then showed the Prince the two servants who were to wait upon him, and from whom he could request all his needs. The most pressing matter then was to put him to bed. The two Governors were also led into the same chamber, at a sufficient distance from that of the Prince.

These proposals made the Governor shudder. He realized that the King loved neither his subjects nor his soldiers, and that he should not expect any better fate for himself. The kindest thing he could think was that this change in fortune was beginning to disturb the mind of **Antaeus**. He resolved to hide from everyone, without exception, his annotated letter and the King's secret order, until he had consulted with himself and himself alone. With this intent, he kept both on his person. But he had the promise of reinforcements published, even though he knew it to be false, because it could inspire his garrison with a courage they needed even more than if it had been true.

Half an hour later, among the workers of the besiegers, an arrow was picked up from among several others that were frequently shot at them. A note had been spotted under the wings <note>The fletching or feathers of the arrow.</note> of this arrow, which was carried to **Cherès**, who was nearby. He found there these three words: *succor shortly* <note>original: "secours dans peu."</note>. Thus, to forestall him, seeing that the Governor sent him no word, he concluded with the Carthaginian officers the plan for a general and sudden assault, which he held ready for this twelfth day. The play of the batteries <note>The coordinated firing of siege engines or early artillery.</note> was so universal and so terrifying

Although they had only agricultural tools for weapons, they harassed these beaten troops strangely as they marched with a hurried pace, causing them to lose many more men. Giscon followed them closely, hoping to defeat the enemy again and enter Carthage by taking advantage of the discouragement that this sight would surely cause in the besieging army.

It was also on this occasion that the Senate, to satisfy the eager demands of all the people and the desires of its absent Prince, pronounced a general and unconditional amnesty <note>Original: "abolition" — here meaning a formal pardon or wiping away of past legal charges or failures.</note> in favor of the victorious Giscon.

Meanwhile, the same Senate, which exercised sovereign authority alone in the absence of its Prince, sent a grand delegation to Cherès the very next day. The Council yielded, after some difficulties, to the intentions of Chérès. Scarcely had they set foot on land when a herald came to offer peace to Chérès on behalf of Antaeus. He told him that the King his master promised to lift the siege of Carthage at the very moment his son was returned to him. Chérès replied coldly that the siege of Carthage was already lifted; and that it was the <term>Tingitan Army</term> <note>The forces of King Antaeus, originating from Tingis (modern Tangier).</note> which was currently besieged and which ought to ask for quarter <note>To "ask for quarter" is a historical military term meaning to beg for one's life to be spared by a victor.</note>: But that the Carthaginians, having no desire to abuse their advantage, required of the King above all else that he consent to release immediately his prisoners whom he had bound in irons, and to arrange them with their hands and feet free between the vanguard of his army and the city walls.

That for his part, he would send word to ask Gisco <note>French: Giscon; a common name for high-ranking Carthaginian military leaders.</note>, or the Governor of Carthage, to arrange in the same manner outside the open gate the prisoners of the Carthaginians, accompanied by a suitable escort from the garrison. That then, without counting one side or the other, they would allow those who chose one fate or the other to return under the banners of their Prince or remain with the opposing party.

The victors and the new prisoners followed them with their eyes; and Cherès, passing along the ranks, commanded his men in a loud voice not to offer him any assistance, as such help would be an act of cowardice. He had, however, taken for defensive arms that day only a helmet and a breastplate of a very light form, both intended more for ornament than for a combat which he had little expected; and he even had the generosity, or perhaps the pride, not to mention this disadvantage to Antaeus. But having closely observed the knight and the horse he was to fight, and willingly yielding to them the advantage of raw strength over himself and his own mount, he dared to rely on the superiority of his skill and on the flexibility of his horse. 

The beginning of this combat appeared to be, on the part of Cherès, nothing more than a defense against the blows of Antaeus. The King, unable to land any blow on his adversary, tried to strike the head of Cherès's horse; but Cherès protected the animal's head as carefully as his own. What surprised the King even more was that it seemed—as was indeed the case—that Cherès was avoiding wounding the King's horse with the same care he took to prevent the King from wounding his own. Thus returning his focus to the knight, the King perceived that Cherès was retreating; he believed this was due to fear, or at least due to the impossibility his enemy saw in finding an opening <note>original: "un jour," literally "a day," referring to a gap or joint in the armor plates where a weapon could penetrate.</note> through the suit of armor with which the King was covered. The establishment of **Tygee** in his states and the return of the recluses of the **Hesperides** to **Carthage** follow so naturally from everything we have just set forth that, if this portion of our history were a poem, we would be obliged to end it here. Even a historian typically shortens the narrative of peaceful situations, which are the eventual outcome of great national upheavals and the tumultuous events of war. The longest spans of time passed without trouble become the shortest in his work. The readers’ attention is rarely sustained except by the divisions or revolutions of Empires, or at least by conquests which, while making a Prince or a People famous, presuppose the desolation of many others. Thus, one can always say: Happy the country, and happy the age, whose history is not entertaining. <note>A play on the common adage "Happy is the nation that has no history," suggesting that peace is better for the people than for the reader's amusement.</note>

The false Sethos, upon receiving this response, was more pleased with it than Osoroth had believed. It suited this impostor little to act by way of negotiation. However strong he might be, not only by the ease and boldness of his genius but also by the advantage he had of being raised alongside Sethos, he was not ignorant of the enormous difference between falsehood and truth. He knew well that the slightest mistake—however inevitable even the largest errors may be—causes a false premise to collapse. He aspired instead to a conquest favored at first by public error, which would then place him above the need for proof. # BOOK X.

The arrival of Cherès in Egypt had, at the moment he landed, brought the impostor Afarès to the foot of Bubastis <note>An ancient city in the eastern Nile Delta, famous as a center for the worship of the goddess Bastet.</note>, situated inland about ten leagues <note>A league was a unit of distance roughly equal to three miles or 4.8 kilometers.</note> from Heropolis. Cherès, having directed his army to cross the Nile and its canals over bridges or in boats, encamped a short distance on this side of the enemy. 

Afarès felt the natural superiority of a man who had, so to speak, conquered nature itself by completing the entire circumnavigation of Africa; who had bestowed customs and laws upon all the Barbarians of its coasts; and who had finally, through his courage and wisdom, pacified the two greatest empires of the Mediterranean. Afarès did not believe himself destined to end so many successes or to erase such glory in a single battle and by a single defeat. He judged it more prudent to limit himself to a defensive posture and to wait for whatever time and circumstances might provide. 

Thus, from the first day he was certain of the course Cherès was taking, he had begun to tighten his camp and to fortify it with every kind of entrenchment that his industry and the layout of the terrain could help him devise. Furthermore, as he was master of all the territory behind him reaching as far as the Red Sea, he had maintained a wide entrance on that side, under the pretext of receiving the reinforcements he would summon—not only from Heropolis and his fleet, but from the coasts of Arabia—should the siege prove long. But in reality, as he possessed more foresight than these Barbarians <note>Referring to the nomadic or mercenary Arab forces supporting him.</note>, he was preparing for himself and for them a prompt and easy exit, in case his resistance was forced to yield to his adversary's good fortune.

Cherès, arriving before Bubastis, comforted himself regarding the impossibility of offering battle to the Impostor and the difficulty of forcing him from his entrenchments; he took solace in the consideration that his presence at least relieved the City of any further attack: for not a single besieger now set foot outside his palisades. He even tried to lure them out by an apparent disorder. He spread his forces out much further than he had initially; and counting on his own vigilance, as well as on sentries who were all the more attentive because they made little show of being so, he spent five days and five nights with all his troops under tents or canvas, in a place well-suited for giving battle, if the enemy had wished it.

This lure having not succeeded, his entire army—which he had wanted to spare from an exploit that could have been bloody and murderous—pressed him of its own accord to lead them against the enemy, who had carried their fear of attack too far to be very fearsome in their defense. Things were at this point when a Herald came to tell Cherès on behalf of the false Sethos that he was ready to lift the siege of Bubastis and return to his fleet, if Cherès himself withdrew to a distance of two days' march: because the Arabs could not risk the movements necessary for their retreat in the presence, or even in the vicinity, of an enemy army.
