Cherès, in the presence of his army, gave a brief two-word response to this Herald: "Tell your leader that I have no wish to retreat, and that I should be very sorry if he himself were to retreat." These few words, when reported back to Asarès, did not fail to terrify him. Because of the high opinion he held of Cherès's intelligence and resources, he feared that he had devised some stratagem to surprise him in the midst of his own entrenchments. Soon after, word came from within the City that, from the height of the towers, a muffled movement could be observed in the enemy camp, which they were disguising as much as possible. Cherès, having gone to observe it himself, judged that the besiegers were preparing to retreat during the following night. He understood that it was not in their interest to waste their time before a city they no longer intended to attack, nor to remain pointlessly so far from Herôpolis, their base of operations <term>place d'armes: a fortified location used as a headquarters and assembly point for an army</term>. Thus, he prepared to follow them. He was careful not to disturb them as they left their camp, and he pretended to be unaware of their departure throughout its duration.

The following day at the break of dawn, he found himself with his six thousand horsemen at the rear of a very numerous army; however, this enemy force consisted almost entirely of infantry, as it had been intended for conducting a siege. Cherès—who saw no better position from which he could more calmly await the succession of the Kingdom of Memphis <note>The ancient capital of Egypt; Sethos is the rightful heir to this throne.</note> when it should fall to him—replied to the King that he would have the honor of benefiting from his kindness until the service of Egypt, and especially of Memphis, his true homeland, called him elsewhere. Space was made in the six vessels for some Ethiopians, who were to find their own ships at the White Port <note>original: "le port blanc" — likely Leuke Kome, a major Red Sea trading port.</note> where they conducted trade, and who departed with the same regret as the Islanders. Then, leaving Beon with the title of Commandant, and under the counsel of several skilled Officers whom he had known in the past, and who no longer recognized him; he instructed him to receive and station in the quarters he assigned the auxiliary troops that were expected to arrive. After which, accompanied by only a few people, he went toward the sea coasts to inspect them, and to gain, if possible, with his own eyes, some knowledge of the enemy fleet.

It was natural to begin this inspection at the place where Pemphos was camped; all the more so because this Prince had chosen the part of the shore most devoid of Fortresses, and where the nature of the terrain made the approach the easiest. His tent was immediately on the seashore; and it was surrounded at a distance by an Army of six thousand men. His mother, to console him for the troubles she gave him elsewhere, had conferred upon him the title of Commandant while nevertheless subjecting him to a Council. But the vivacity of this young Prince, and the experience he had acquired in his travels—which he knew how to use to his advantage—had already changed this title into reality. However, as soon as he learned that the **Conservator** <note>The "Conservator" (Conservateur) is the official title held by the protagonist, Sethos, while in disguise as Cherès, signifying his role as a protector of the state</note> was arriving at his outer lines, he sent a deputation to him, through which he explained that, as he did not believe he should leave his post so close to nightfall, he awaited him at the entrance of his tent to hand over the command. Pemphos took charge of distributing them among the maritime cities until such time as buyers should come for them. After this, he went to the camp of the Conservator, who had been the first to return there. Cherès, having dismissed all his troops from there with appropriate praise and rewards, prepared after three days to return to the Capital with the two Princes; followed by the officers and companies whose rank attached them to the three of them.

They made these verses contribute greatly to the effect of an illusion, which was further aided by the admirable art of the actors, by a very fine sense of perspective, by a grand management of lighting, and above all by the disposition of the Spectatress, for whom love was then the most powerful of enchanters. ->CHORUS OF THE EGYPTIAN PEOPLES.<-

O Gods, whose homeland Egypt once dared to call herself,
In our misfortunes, your glory is tarnished.
Upon us, and upon our Kings—your sons and successors—
Pour out the sweetness of your joyful reign.

->T H E C O R Y P H A E U S<- <term>Coryphaeus</term> <note>The leader of the chorus who speaks or sings individually, acting as a bridge between the audience and the performers.</note>

Who is this Hero whom my eyes
Can barely perceive from here?
He emerges from the very bosom of the Gods
And his path leads him toward us.
This long succession of Kings,
Who clear a path for him among them,
In his bearing and in his deeds
Recognize their own living image;
They expect that his courage,
In these places as dear to them now as in the past,
Will, after a long storm,
Bring Peace and the Laws back to life.

"No," she said, "I wish to know my fate, and I even dare to believe it will be happy." She was told she would soon receive satisfaction.

In effect, she was led into a booth as dark as the first by a path she believed to be the same. The concept of this second scene was to represent the struggle taking place in the soul of Sethos between love and heroic virtue, portrayed by two characters: one representing the <term>Man</term> <note>Representing Sethos’s personal desires and human emotions.</note> and the other the <term>Hero</term> <note>Representing his public duty, royal obligations, and stoic discipline.</note>. Both had the height and gait of Sethos; and by means of their imperceptible masks, they bore a perfect resemblance to his face. Furthermore, some steel blades or strips of parchment skillfully placed at the level of the lips gave them the very tone of his voice. * . The Priests of Heliopolis excelled in these sorts of scenes, which possessed something of those images—mingled with impossibility or contradiction—that dreams often present to those with great troubles in their minds or great passions in their hearts. The solitude in which they had kept the <term>Consultants</term> <note>Seekers or initiates who came to the temple for guidance.</note>, the spectacles they had already paraded before their eyes (some of which inspired terror), and the mild narcotics they had administered during their fast, had rendered them susceptible by de—

Immediately, as darkness spread everywhere, she was transported in a machine <term>machine: a stage device or hidden elevator common in 18th-century "mystery" theater to create the illusion of magic or supernatural movement</term> made specifically for this purpose—which also held her two conductors—to the apartment she had been given next to the Temple. It was located precisely above their Theater; and as this transport was always carried out in profound darkness, the Seekers <note>original: "Consultans"; those participating in the initiation or seeking an oracular experience</note>, when the light was restored to them, found themselves in this apartment without knowing how they had re-entered it, and without being able to understand how they had returned from so far away in so little time.

Indeed, they showed her through a shutter <term>jalousie: a slatted blind or window covering that allows one to see out while remaining hidden</term> in her room a table magnificently served in a neighboring room, and the same company that had received her waiting without impatience to see what her wishes might be. Mnevie, who possessed a politeness and a kindness without equal, replied to her guides that she asked for only half an hour to recover and compose herself; and she requested that the Priest go and tell the company immediately that they were doing her the honor of waiting for her. She added, however, before he left, that being unable to leave the King her father alone any longer, she would depart immediately after the meal she was about to take with the Priests and Priestesses; and thus, she asked that they please notify her officers and her women <note>meaning her ladies-in-waiting and attendants</note>.

Upon leaving the room where she was after half an hour to pass into the other, she embraced with great marks of friendship and gratitude the Priestess, who, in addition to the constancy of her conversation and her consolations, had served her for twelve days like a servant; and while giving her her portrait encrusted with diamonds, she promised a more substantial gift for the Temple of Heliopolis <note>A major religious center in ancient Egypt, known as the "City of the Sun"</note>.

### B O O K X.
<page-num>365</page-num>

As soon as the Princess—escorted after the meal by the entire company that had eaten with her—had climbed back into her carriage, her Nurse, sitting beside her just as she had been on the way there, said to her: "Ah, Madam! How impatient I was to see you again, to give you happy news that you perhaps did not learn in the retreat from which you have just emerged. Your Lover, recognized for who he truly is, is preparing to come to Tanis ready to marry you; he is freed from all obstacles, and particularly from the difficulty that would have been raised by the King." Immediately, this woman gave her such a favorable account of this event that the Princess regarded as mere fictions all the sinister things that had been announced to her by the answers <note>Referring to the oracular or ritual responses Mnevie received while in the temple's "retreat."</note> she had just received. But to help the Reader understand the reason for this confidence, it is necessary that we return to Sethos, still bearing the name of Cherès, in the camp where we left him victorious over the Arabs and master of the person of Afarès, his former slave who had usurped his name.

THE Conservator <term>Conservateur: a high-ranking official or priest in this context, often responsible for the preservation of laws and the initiation of princes</term>, upon leaving this camp for Memphis, had placed his captive in a carriage where he was alone and seated, with no other discomfort than seeing no one and receiving light only through the top of the wooden planks that enclosed him. There, he was served during the breaks in the journey without a word being said to him. During the night while they were camped, Cherès had a bed laid out in this same carriage long enough to accommodate him, and had the prisoner watched while locked inside by sentries who worked in shifts. Having arrived in Memphis <note>The ancient capital of Egypt and the seat of the royal court in this narrative.</note>, he went first to the King’s Palace, and presenting to him the two Princes whom he was bringing back, he said to him before a numerous Court: That besides an infinite number of proofs of courage and prudence they had given, he was indebted for his life to Prince Beon, who had parried a saber stroke aimed at him by the enemy General; and that the Kingdom and all Egypt owed to Prince Pemphos the burning of the Arab fleet. He added that regarding the captive he brought with him, he believed it important to have a large platform erected before the palace gate: That there, in the presence of all the People, the captive should undergo interrogations put to him by Cherès <note>The name Sethos adopted while in disguise to hide his true identity from his stepmother.</note> his vanquisher, who had also been present at the siege of Coptos where Sethos had disappeared: That he would be assisted in this examination by Priests who had followed Sethos from his earliest childhood until the end of his Initiation <note>Refers to the rigorous Egyptian mystery trials Sethos underwent in the earlier books.</note>: and that those of the Lords present, who had witnessed the entire ministry of Queen Nephté, would form their doubts or communicate their insights on this subject. 

The Queen, who feared for many reasons the consequences of this disclosure, cried out at once that it was useless, and that it was enough to shut Sethos in a perpetual prison; a punishment too mild, she added, for his revolt, and for the evils he had caused Egypt. It is for that reason, Madam, replied the Conservator <term>Conservateur: a high-ranking official responsible for the preservation of laws and the education of the royal family</term>, that the criminal must be submitted to a public judgment, which by condemning the person will perhaps justify the name. The King, full of the obligations he owed to Cherès, spoke loudly in agreement with him; and he added that he was turning this matter over to him to pursue,

One will not be surprised that Queen Daluca, having lost her rank against her will through the voluntary abdication of her husband, had fled to the back of her apartments. But she took her despair further. Seeing herself fallen from her past power, and above all from her future power which she valued much more; persuaded, moreover, that Sethos was going to take vengeance for the destruction she had once attempted against him, and for all the vexations <note>In this context, "vexations" refers to the political harassment and abuses of power she committed while in favor.</note> she had exercised during the course of her ministry and her influence; she took justice into her own hands by swallowing a poison that she believed to be more violent and more rapid than it actually was. But when he was certain that Daluca could not escape the death she had brought upon herself, he felt himself free to give a greater effort to his generosity; and above all to clear from all suspicion and jealousy the title of Conservator <note>A title meaning "Protector" or "Guardian of the Laws."</note>, which love of the Homeland and the choice of all the Kings of Egypt made him prefer in the depths of his soul to that of King of Memphis.
